# Dependency Scanning — Policy and Exception Management

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Dependency Scanning — Policy and Exception Management" within the navigation topic "Dependency Scanning" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Ignore Policies. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Ignore policies determine how selected findings are treated during reporting or automated enforcement. They may be needed for verified false positives, accepted risks, or findings awaiting a controlled remediation. An exception does not remove the underlying vulnerability or make the affected artifact secure. Use the narrowest supported scope, document the finding identifier and reason, assign an accountable owner, obtain approval, and review exceptions periodically. Validate the ignore configuration against the installed Trivy version and confirm that unrelated findings remain visible.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Policy exceptions: explain the scope of an exception, how it affects findings, approval and ownership requirements, expiration or review, and how to avoid hiding unrelated security risks.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

## 4. Practical DevOps Workflow

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "Dependency Scanning — Policy and Exception Management", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "Dependency Scanning", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. The engineer should also understand the limitations of the check and know when additional application, infrastructure, or runtime security validation is necessary.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Trivy troubleshooting begins by separating scanner execution problems from actual security findings. Common causes include an incorrect target path, unsupported file formats, registry authentication failures, network or proxy problems, unavailable vulnerability databases, permission errors, and invalid command options. Collect the command, scanner version, target identity, exit status, and relevant error output without exposing secrets. Verify the target independently, check database and registry connectivity, and repeat the scan after correcting the cause. A failed or incomplete scan must never be interpreted as a clean security result.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Severity classification communicates the assessed seriousness of a security finding. Trivy reports severity values such as UNKNOWN, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, and CRITICAL where supported by the underlying vulnerability information. Severity is an important prioritization signal, but it is not a complete measure of business risk. A production policy should define thresholds, ownership, escalation, and exception approval rather than treating every finding with the same operational response.

Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "Container Image Scanning — Filesystem and Dependency Analysis", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "Container Image Scanning", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. The engineer should also understand the limitations of the check and know when additional application, infrastructure, or runtime security validation is necessary.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

## 4. Practical DevOps Workflow

Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. ## 2. Technical Explanation

Severity classification communicates the assessed seriousness of a security finding. Severity is an important prioritization signal, but it is not a complete measure of business risk. Exploitability, exposure, affected runtime paths, compensating controls, and asset importance also matter. A production policy should define thresholds, ownership, escalation, and exception approval rather than treating every finding with the same operational response.

## 2. Technical Explanation

A Software Bill of Materials is an inventory of software components contained in an application or artifact. For example, trivy image --format cyclonedx --output sbom.json my-app:latest generates a CycloneDX output for an accessible image. Associate the SBOM with the exact image digest and release identifier. An SBOM is an inventory, not a guarantee that the listed software is secure.

# Container Image Scanning — Remediation and Verification

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Container Image Scanning — Remediation and Verification" within the navigation topic "Container Image Scanning" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Vulnerability Remediation. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Vulnerability remediation removes or reduces the risk represented by a security finding. Begin by confirming the affected package, installed version, advisory identifier, and available fixed version. Determine whether the package is direct or transitive and identify the dependency or base image responsible. Update the appropriate dependency or rebuild from a patched base image, run automated tests, rebuild the final artifact, and scan it again. Do not close a finding merely because a source manifest changed; verify that the released image contains the corrected package version.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Remediation: explain how to identify the affected component, select a supported fixed version, evaluate compatibility, test the change, rebuild the artifact, and verify the result with a fresh scan.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

## 4. Practical DevOps Workflow

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "Container Image Scanning — Remediation and Verification", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "Container Image Scanning", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. The engineer should also understand the limitations of the check and know when additional application, infrastructure, or runtime security validation is necessary.

# Container Image Scanning — Troubleshooting and Diagnostics

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Container Image Scanning — Troubleshooting and Diagnostics" within the navigation topic "Container Image Scanning" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Troubleshooting. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Trivy troubleshooting begins by separating scanner execution problems from actual security findings. Common causes include an incorrect target path, unsupported file formats, registry authentication failures, network or proxy problems, unavailable vulnerability databases, permission errors, and invalid command options. Collect the command, scanner version, target identity, exit status, and relevant error output without exposing secrets. Verify the target independently, check database and registry connectivity, and repeat the scan after correcting the cause. A failed or incomplete scan must never be interpreted as a clean security result.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Troubleshooting: explain the symptoms, likely technical causes, evidence to collect, diagnostic commands, safe corrective actions, and the validation required before closing the issue.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Severity classification communicates the assessed seriousness of a security finding. Trivy reports severity values such as UNKNOWN, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, and CRITICAL where supported by the underlying vulnerability information. Severity is an important prioritization signal, but it is not a complete measure of business risk. Exploitability, exposure, affected runtime paths, compensating controls, and asset importance also matter. A production policy should define thresholds, ownership, escalation, and exception approval rather than treating every finding with the same operational response.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

# Container Image Scanning — Security Scanning Fundamentals — Container Image Scanning [stage-7-topic-5-section-17]

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Container Image Scanning — Security Scanning Fundamentals — Container Image Scanning [stage-7-topic-5-section-17]" within the navigation topic "Container Image Scanning" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Container Image Scanning. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Container image scanning inspects an image for supported operating-system packages, language dependencies, vulnerabilities, secrets, and other enabled security checks. Run trivy image my-app:latest to inspect an accessible image. Trivy analyzes image metadata and filesystem layers to identify installed components and match them against available security information. Registry authentication and network access may be required for private images. Production pipelines should scan the final built image and record its immutable digest so the artifact that passed scanning is the same artifact promoted to deployment.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Container image analysis: explain image identification, layer and package discovery, registry access, vulnerability matching, image digest tracking, and the difference between image scanning and runtime security.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

# CVE Database — Security Scanning Fundamentals

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "CVE Database — Security Scanning Fundamentals" within the navigation topic "CVE Database" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of CVE Database. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Trivy uses vulnerability information from its configured databases and advisory sources to match identified software packages with known security issues. CVE identifiers provide a common reference for publicly disclosed vulnerabilities, while package ecosystems may also publish their own advisory identifiers. Database freshness matters because new advisories and fixed-version information appear over time. A scan using stale data can miss recently disclosed issues. Teams should monitor database update failures, retain scanner and database context where available, and distinguish database access failures from a genuinely clean scan.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Database and cache management: explain database sources, update behavior, local cache considerations, network dependencies, freshness, and how stale security information affects results.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "CVE Database — Container Image Assessment" within the navigation topic "CVE Database" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of CVE Database. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Trivy uses vulnerability information from its configured databases and advisory sources to match identified software packages with known security issues. CVE identifiers provide a common reference for publicly disclosed vulnerabilities, while package ecosystems may also publish their own advisory identifiers. Database freshness matters because new advisories and fixed-version information appear over time. A scan using stale data can miss recently disclosed issues. Teams should monitor database update failures, retain scanner and database context where available, and distinguish database access failures from a genuinely clean scan.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Database and cache management: explain database sources, update behavior, local cache considerations, network dependencies, freshness, and how stale security information affects results.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

## 4. Practical DevOps Workflow

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "CVE Database — Container Image Assessment", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "CVE Database", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. The engineer should also understand the limitations of the check and know when additional application, infrastructure, or runtime security validation is necessary.

## Section Reference

# CVE Database — Secret Detection

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "CVE Database — Secret Detection" within the navigation topic "CVE Database" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Secret Scanning. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Secret scanning searches supported files and artifacts for values that may represent credentials or sensitive authentication material. Examples include API tokens, passwords, cloud keys, and private keys. A typical filesystem command is trivy fs --scanners secret . Detection results should be handled as confidential security data because reports may reveal sensitive locations or values. If a real credential is exposed, remove the exposure where appropriate, revoke or rotate the credential, investigate possible misuse, and move future secrets into an approved secrets manager.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Database and cache management: explain database sources, update behavior, local cache considerations, network dependencies, freshness, and how stale security information affects results.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

## 4. Practical DevOps Workflow

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "CVE Database — Secret Detection", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "CVE Database", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. The engineer should also understand the limitations of the check and know when additional application, infrastructure, or runtime security validation is necessary.

# CVE Database — SBOM and Supply Chain Security

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "CVE Database — SBOM and Supply Chain Security" within the navigation topic "CVE Database" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of SBOM Generation. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

A Software Bill of Materials is an inventory of software components contained in an application or artifact. It supports vulnerability investigations, license review, supply-chain visibility, and impact analysis when a package becomes unsafe. Trivy can generate supported SBOM formats for scanned targets. For example, trivy image --format cyclonedx --output sbom.json my-app:latest generates a CycloneDX output for an accessible image. Associate the SBOM with the exact image digest and release identifier. An SBOM is an inventory, not a guarantee that the listed software is secure.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Database and cache management: explain database sources, update behavior, local cache considerations, network dependencies, freshness, and how stale security information affects results.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

## 4. Practical DevOps Workflow

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "CVE Database — SBOM and Supply Chain Security", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "CVE Database", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. The engineer should also understand the limitations of the check and know when additional application, infrastructure, or runtime security validation is necessary.

If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "CVE Database — Remediation and Verification", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "CVE Database", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. The engineer should also understand the limitations of the check and know when additional application, infrastructure, or runtime security validation is necessary.

# CVE Database — Troubleshooting and Diagnostics

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "CVE Database — Troubleshooting and Diagnostics" within the navigation topic "CVE Database" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of CVE Database. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Trivy uses vulnerability information from its configured databases and advisory sources to match identified software packages with known security issues. CVE identifiers provide a common reference for publicly disclosed vulnerabilities, while package ecosystems may also publish their own advisory identifiers. Database freshness matters because new advisories and fixed-version information appear over time. A scan using stale data can miss recently disclosed issues. Teams should monitor database update failures, retain scanner and database context where available, and distinguish database access failures from a genuinely clean scan.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Database and cache management: explain database sources, update behavior, local cache considerations, network dependencies, freshness, and how stale security information affects results.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

## 4. Practical DevOps Workflow

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. # Severity Classification — Security Scanning Fundamentals

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Severity Classification — Security Scanning Fundamentals" within the navigation topic "Severity Classification" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Severity Classification. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Severity classification communicates the assessed seriousness of a security finding. Trivy reports severity values such as UNKNOWN, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, and CRITICAL where supported by the underlying vulnerability information. Severity is an important prioritization signal, but it is not a complete measure of business risk. Exploitability, exposure, affected runtime paths, compensating controls, and asset importance also matter. A production policy should define thresholds, ownership, escalation, and exception approval rather than treating every finding with the same operational response.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Severity interpretation: explain how severity is represented, how teams should interpret the rating, why severity is not identical to exploitability, and how risk-based policy should be applied.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

## 4. Practical DevOps Workflow

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

# Severity Classification — Misconfiguration Detection

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Severity Classification — Misconfiguration Detection" within the navigation topic "Severity Classification" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Severity Classification. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Severity classification communicates the assessed seriousness of a security finding. Trivy reports severity values such as UNKNOWN, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, and CRITICAL where supported by the underlying vulnerability information. Severity is an important prioritization signal, but it is not a complete measure of business risk. Exploitability, exposure, affected runtime paths, compensating controls, and asset importance also matter. A production policy should define thresholds, ownership, escalation, and exception approval rather than treating every finding with the same operational response.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Severity interpretation: explain how severity is represented, how teams should interpret the rating, why severity is not identical to exploitability, and how risk-based policy should be applied.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

## 4. Practical DevOps Workflow

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "Severity Classification — Misconfiguration Detection", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "Severity Classification", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. The engineer should also understand the limitations of the check and know when additional application, infrastructure, or runtime security validation is necessary.

# Severity Classification — Secret Detection

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Severity Classification — Secret Detection" within the navigation topic "Severity Classification" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Secret Scanning. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Secret scanning searches supported files and artifacts for values that may represent credentials or sensitive authentication material. Examples include API tokens, passwords, cloud keys, and private keys. A typical filesystem command is trivy fs --scanners secret . Detection results should be handled as confidential security data because reports may reveal sensitive locations or values. If a real credential is exposed, remove the exposure where appropriate, revoke or rotate the credential, investigate possible misuse, and move future secrets into an approved secrets manager.

# Severity Classification — SBOM and Supply Chain Security

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Severity Classification — SBOM and Supply Chain Security" within the navigation topic "Severity Classification" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of SBOM Generation. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

A Software Bill of Materials is an inventory of software components contained in an application or artifact. It supports vulnerability investigations, license review, supply-chain visibility, and impact analysis when a package becomes unsafe. Trivy can generate supported SBOM formats for scanned targets. For example, trivy image --format cyclonedx --output sbom.json my-app:latest generates a CycloneDX output for an accessible image. Associate the SBOM with the exact image digest and release identifier. An SBOM is an inventory, not a guarantee that the listed software is secure.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Severity interpretation: explain how severity is represented, how teams should interpret the rating, why severity is not identical to exploitability, and how risk-based policy should be applied.

Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Misconfiguration scanning evaluates supported infrastructure and application configuration files against security checks. Trivy config . can inspect supported files in the selected directory. Checks may identify insecure settings such as excessive permissions, unsafe exposure, or weak workload configuration. Findings should be reviewed with the affected resource, rule identifier, severity, and recommended remediation. The scanner evaluates the configuration it can discover; it does not automatically prove that deployed infrastructure has the same state or that runtime controls are effective.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Technical implementation: explain the purpose of this subject, its inputs and outputs, the internal processing sequence, relevant Trivy behavior, practical DevOps usage, validation, and operational limitations.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

## 4. Practical DevOps Workflow

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "Misconfiguration Scanning — Vulnerability Intelligence and CVEs", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "Misconfiguration Scanning", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. The engineer should also understand the limitations of the check and know when additional application, infrastructure, or runtime security validation is necessary.

# Misconfiguration Scanning — Severity and Risk Evaluation

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Misconfiguration Scanning — Severity and Risk Evaluation" within the navigation topic "Misconfiguration Scanning" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Severity Classification. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Severity classification communicates the assessed seriousness of a security finding. Trivy reports severity values such as UNKNOWN, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, and CRITICAL where supported by the underlying vulnerability information. Severity is an important prioritization signal, but it is not a complete measure of business risk. Exploitability, exposure, affected runtime paths, compensating controls, and asset importance also matter. A production policy should define thresholds, ownership, escalation, and exception approval rather than treating every finding with the same operational response.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Severity interpretation: explain how severity is represented, how teams should interpret the rating, why severity is not identical to exploitability, and how risk-based policy should be applied.

# Misconfiguration Scanning — Secret Detection

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Misconfiguration Scanning — Secret Detection" within the navigation topic "Misconfiguration Scanning" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Secret Scanning. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Secret scanning searches supported files and artifacts for values that may represent credentials or sensitive authentication material. Examples include API tokens, passwords, cloud keys, and private keys. A typical filesystem command is trivy fs --scanners secret . Detection results should be handled as confidential security data because reports may reveal sensitive locations or values. If a real credential is exposed, remove the exposure where appropriate, revoke or rotate the credential, investigate possible misuse, and move future secrets into an approved secrets manager.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Secret handling: explain the sensitive data involved, detection limitations, the risk of exposure, safe investigation, credential rotation, and prevention of future leaks.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. # Misconfiguration Scanning — SBOM and Supply Chain Security

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Misconfiguration Scanning — SBOM and Supply Chain Security" within the navigation topic "Misconfiguration Scanning" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

A Software Bill of Materials is an inventory of software components contained in an application or artifact. It supports vulnerability investigations, license review, supply-chain visibility, and impact analysis when a package becomes unsafe. Trivy can generate supported SBOM formats for scanned targets. For example, trivy image --format cyclonedx --output sbom.json my-app:latest generates a CycloneDX output for an accessible image. Associate the SBOM with the exact image digest and release identifier. An SBOM is an inventory, not a guarantee that the listed software is secure.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Software inventory: explain component identification, package metadata, SBOM formats, artifact association, and how the inventory supports vulnerability and license investigations.

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "Misconfiguration Scanning — Troubleshooting and Diagnostics", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "Misconfiguration Scanning", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. The engineer should also understand the limitations of the check and know when additional application, infrastructure, or runtime security validation is necessary.

# Misconfiguration Scanning — Production Security Workflow

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Misconfiguration Scanning — Production Security Workflow" within the navigation topic "Misconfiguration Scanning" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Severity Classification. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Severity classification communicates the assessed seriousness of a security finding. Trivy reports severity values such as UNKNOWN, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, and CRITICAL where supported by the underlying vulnerability information. Severity is an important prioritization signal, but it is not a complete measure of business risk. Exploitability, exposure, affected runtime paths, compensating controls, and asset importance also matter. A production policy should define thresholds, ownership, escalation, and exception approval rather than treating every finding with the same operational response.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Severity interpretation: explain how severity is represented, how teams should interpret the rating, why severity is not identical to exploitability, and how risk-based policy should be applied.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

## 4. Practical DevOps Workflow

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

# Kubernetes Configuration Scanning — Security Scanning Fundamentals

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Kubernetes Configuration Scanning — Security Scanning Fundamentals" within the navigation topic "Kubernetes Configuration Scanning" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Kubernetes Configuration Scanning. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Kubernetes configuration scanning examines supported manifests and deployment definitions for security weaknesses. Important areas include container privilege settings, host namespace usage, privilege escalation, capabilities, resource exposure, service accounts, and security context configuration. Trivy config can scan supported manifest files, while image scanning separately evaluates the referenced container image. These checks answer different questions: a secure manifest can still reference a vulnerable image, and a secure image can still run with excessive privileges. Live cluster security requires additional runtime and admission controls.

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "Kubernetes Configuration Scanning — Severity and Risk Evaluation", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "Kubernetes Configuration Scanning", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. The engineer should also understand the limitations of the check and know when additional application, infrastructure, or runtime security validation is necessary.

The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Misconfiguration scanning evaluates supported infrastructure and application configuration files against security checks. Trivy config . can inspect supported files in the selected directory. Checks may identify insecure settings such as excessive permissions, unsafe exposure, or weak workload configuration. Findings should be reviewed with the affected resource, rule identifier, severity, and recommended remediation. The scanner evaluates the configuration it can discover; it does not automatically prove that deployed infrastructure has the same state or that runtime controls are effective.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

# Kubernetes Configuration Scanning — Secret Detection

This section explains "Kubernetes Configuration Scanning — Secret Detection" within the navigation topic "Kubernetes Configuration Scanning" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Secret scanning searches supported files and artifacts for values that may represent credentials or sensitive authentication material. Examples include API tokens, passwords, cloud keys, and private keys. A typical filesystem command is trivy fs --scanners secret . Detection results should be handled as confidential security data because reports may reveal sensitive locations or values. If a real credential is exposed, remove the exposure where appropriate, revoke or rotate the credential, investigate possible misuse, and move future secrets into an approved secrets manager.

## 2. Technical Explanation

A Software Bill of Materials is an inventory of software components contained in an application or artifact. It supports vulnerability investigations, license review, supply-chain visibility, and impact analysis when a package becomes unsafe. Trivy can generate supported SBOM formats for scanned targets. For example, trivy image --format cyclonedx --output sbom.json my-app:latest generates a CycloneDX output for an accessible image. Associate the SBOM with the exact image digest and release identifier. An SBOM is an inventory, not a guarantee that the listed software is secure.

# Kubernetes Configuration Scanning — Production Security Workflow

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Kubernetes Configuration Scanning — Production Security Workflow" within the navigation topic "Kubernetes Configuration Scanning" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Severity Classification. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Severity classification communicates the assessed seriousness of a security finding. Trivy reports severity values such as UNKNOWN, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, and CRITICAL where supported by the underlying vulnerability information. Severity is an important prioritization signal, but it is not a complete measure of business risk. Exploitability, exposure, affected runtime paths, compensating controls, and asset importance also matter. A production policy should define thresholds, ownership, escalation, and exception approval rather than treating every finding with the same operational response.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

# Kubernetes Configuration Scanning — Hands-on Security Exercise

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Kubernetes Configuration Scanning — Hands-on Security Exercise" within the navigation topic "Kubernetes Configuration Scanning" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Kubernetes Configuration Scanning. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Kubernetes configuration scanning examines supported manifests and deployment definitions for security weaknesses. Important areas include container privilege settings, host namespace usage, privilege escalation, capabilities, resource exposure, service accounts, and security context configuration. Trivy config can scan supported manifest files, while image scanning separately evaluates the referenced container image. These checks answer different questions: a secure manifest can still reference a vulnerable image, and a secure image can still run with excessive privileges. Live cluster security requires additional runtime and admission controls.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Kubernetes configuration: explain the relevant Kubernetes resource, its security-sensitive fields, how configuration is evaluated, and what must additionally be checked in the live cluster.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

## 4. Practical DevOps Workflow

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "Kubernetes Configuration Scanning — Hands-on Security Exercise", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "Kubernetes Configuration Scanning", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. The engineer should also understand the limitations of the check and know when additional application, infrastructure, or runtime security validation is necessary.

# Secret Scanning — Security Scanning Fundamentals

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Secret Scanning — Security Scanning Fundamentals" within the navigation topic "Secret Scanning" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Secret Scanning. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Secret scanning searches supported files and artifacts for values that may represent credentials or sensitive authentication material. Examples include API tokens, passwords, cloud keys, and private keys. A typical filesystem command is trivy fs --scanners secret . Detection results should be handled as confidential security data because reports may reveal sensitive locations or values. If a real credential is exposed, remove the exposure where appropriate, revoke or rotate the credential, investigate possible misuse, and move future secrets into an approved secrets manager.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Secret handling: explain the sensitive data involved, detection limitations, the risk of exposure, safe investigation, credential rotation, and prevention of future leaks.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. # Secret Scanning — Misconfiguration Detection

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Secret Scanning — Misconfiguration Detection" within the navigation topic "Secret Scanning" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Secret Scanning. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Secret scanning searches supported files and artifacts for values that may represent credentials or sensitive authentication material. Examples include API tokens, passwords, cloud keys, and private keys. A typical filesystem command is trivy fs --scanners secret . Detection results should be handled as confidential security data because reports may reveal sensitive locations or values. If a real credential is exposed, remove the exposure where appropriate, revoke or rotate the credential, investigate possible misuse, and move future secrets into an approved secrets manager.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Secret handling: explain the sensitive data involved, detection limitations, the risk of exposure, safe investigation, credential rotation, and prevention of future leaks.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

## 4. Practical DevOps Workflow

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "Secret Scanning — Misconfiguration Detection", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "Secret Scanning", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. The engineer should also understand the limitations of the check and know when additional application, infrastructure, or runtime security validation is necessary.

HEADING: SBOM Generation — Security Scanning Fundamentals
