# SBOM Generation — Security Scanning Fundamentals

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "SBOM Generation — Security Scanning Fundamentals" within the navigation topic "SBOM Generation" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of SBOM Generation. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

A Software Bill of Materials is an inventory of software components contained in an application or artifact. It supports vulnerability investigations, license review, supply-chain visibility, and impact analysis when a package becomes unsafe. Trivy can generate supported SBOM formats for scanned targets. For example, trivy image --format cyclonedx --output sbom.json my-app:latest generates a CycloneDX output for an accessible image. Associate the SBOM with the exact image digest and release identifier. An SBOM is an inventory, not a guarantee that the listed software is secure.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Software inventory: explain component identification, package metadata, SBOM formats, artifact association, and how the inventory supports vulnerability and license investigations.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

## 4. Practical DevOps Workflow

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "SBOM Generation — Security Scanning Fundamentals", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "SBOM Generation", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. The engineer should also understand the limitations of the check and know when additional application, infrastructure, or runtime security validation is necessary.

# SBOM Generation — Secret Detection

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "SBOM Generation — Secret Detection" within the navigation topic "SBOM Generation" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Secret Scanning. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Secret scanning searches supported files and artifacts for values that may represent credentials or sensitive authentication material. Examples include API tokens, passwords, cloud keys, and private keys. A typical filesystem command is trivy fs --scanners secret . Detection results should be handled as confidential security data because reports may reveal sensitive locations or values. If a real credential is exposed, remove the exposure where appropriate, revoke or rotate the credential, investigate possible misuse, and move future secrets into an approved secrets manager.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

# SBOM Generation — Policy and Exception Management

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "SBOM Generation — Policy and Exception Management" within the navigation topic "SBOM Generation" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of SBOM Generation. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

A Software Bill of Materials is an inventory of software components contained in an application or artifact. It supports vulnerability investigations, license review, supply-chain visibility, and impact analysis when a package becomes unsafe. Trivy can generate supported SBOM formats for scanned targets. For example, trivy image --format cyclonedx --output sbom.json my-app:latest generates a CycloneDX output for an accessible image. Associate the SBOM with the exact image digest and release identifier. An SBOM is an inventory, not a guarantee that the listed software is secure.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Policy exceptions: explain the scope of an exception, how it affects findings, approval and ownership requirements, expiration or review, and how to avoid hiding unrelated security risks.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

## 4. Practical DevOps Workflow

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "SBOM Generation — Policy and Exception Management", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "SBOM Generation", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. The engineer should also understand the limitations of the check and know when additional application, infrastructure, or runtime security validation is necessary.

# Ignore Policies — Security Scanning Fundamentals

## 1. Overview and Purpose

The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Ignore policies determine how selected findings are treated during reporting or automated enforcement. They may be needed for verified false positives, accepted risks, or findings awaiting a controlled remediation. An exception does not remove the underlying vulnerability or make the affected artifact secure. Use the narrowest supported scope, document the finding identifier and reason, assign an accountable owner, obtain approval, and review exceptions periodically. Validate the ignore configuration against the installed Trivy version and confirm that unrelated findings remain visible.

The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Ignore policies determine how selected findings are treated during reporting or automated enforcement. They may be needed for verified false positives, accepted risks, or findings awaiting a controlled remediation. An exception does not remove the underlying vulnerability or make the affected artifact secure. Use the narrowest supported scope, document the finding identifier and reason, assign an accountable owner, obtain approval, and review exceptions periodically. Validate the ignore configuration against the installed Trivy version and confirm that unrelated findings remain visible.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Policy exceptions: explain the scope of an exception, how it affects findings, approval and ownership requirements, expiration or review, and how to avoid hiding unrelated security risks.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

## 4. Practical DevOps Workflow

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "Ignore Policies — Container Image Assessment", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "Ignore Policies", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. The engineer should also understand the limitations of the check and know when additional application, infrastructure, or runtime security validation is necessary.

# Ignore Policies — Severity and Risk Evaluation

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Ignore Policies — Severity and Risk Evaluation" within the navigation topic "Ignore Policies" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Severity classification communicates the assessed seriousness of a security finding. Trivy reports severity values such as UNKNOWN, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, and CRITICAL where supported by the underlying vulnerability information. Severity is an important prioritization signal, but it is not a complete measure of business risk. Exploitability, exposure, affected runtime paths, compensating controls, and asset importance also matter. A production policy should define thresholds, ownership, escalation, and exception approval rather than treating every finding with the same operational response.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

## 2. Technical Explanation

Kubernetes configuration scanning examines supported manifests and deployment definitions for security weaknesses. Important areas include container privilege settings, host namespace usage, privilege escalation, capabilities, resource exposure, service accounts, and security context configuration. Trivy config can scan supported manifest files, while image scanning separately evaluates the referenced container image. These checks answer different questions: a secure manifest can still reference a vulnerable image, and a secure image can still run with excessive privileges. Live cluster security requires additional runtime and admission controls.

Secret scanning searches supported files and artifacts for values that may represent credentials or sensitive authentication material. Examples include API tokens, passwords, cloud keys, and private keys. A typical filesystem command is trivy fs --scanners secret . Detection results should be handled as confidential security data because reports may reveal sensitive locations or values. If a real credential is exposed, remove the exposure where appropriate, revoke or rotate the credential, investigate possible misuse, and move future secrets into an approved secrets manager.

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Ignore Policies — SBOM and Supply Chain Security" within the navigation topic "Ignore Policies" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

A Software Bill of Materials is an inventory of software components contained in an application or artifact. It supports vulnerability investigations, license review, supply-chain visibility, and impact analysis when a package becomes unsafe. Trivy can generate supported SBOM formats for scanned targets. For example, trivy image --format cyclonedx --output sbom.json my-app:latest generates a CycloneDX output for an accessible image. Associate the SBOM with the exact image digest and release identifier. An SBOM is an inventory, not a guarantee that the listed software is secure.

Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "Ignore Policies — Remediation and Verification", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "Ignore Policies", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. The engineer should also understand the limitations of the check and know when additional application, infrastructure, or runtime security validation is necessary.

# CI Pipeline Integration — Severity and Risk Evaluation

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "CI Pipeline Integration — Severity and Risk Evaluation" within the navigation topic "CI Pipeline Integration" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Severity Classification. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Severity classification communicates the assessed seriousness of a security finding. Trivy reports severity values such as UNKNOWN, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, and CRITICAL where supported by the underlying vulnerability information. Severity is an important prioritization signal, but it is not a complete measure of business risk. Exploitability, exposure, affected runtime paths, compensating controls, and asset importance also matter. A production policy should define thresholds, ownership, escalation, and exception approval rather than treating every finding with the same operational response.

# CI Pipeline Integration — Kubernetes Security Assessment

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "CI Pipeline Integration — Kubernetes Security Assessment" within the navigation topic "CI Pipeline Integration" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Kubernetes Configuration Scanning. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Kubernetes configuration scanning examines supported manifests and deployment definitions for security weaknesses. Important areas include container privilege settings, host namespace usage, privilege escalation, capabilities, resource exposure, service accounts, and security context configuration. Trivy config can scan supported manifest files, while image scanning separately evaluates the referenced container image. These checks answer different questions: a secure manifest can still reference a vulnerable image, and a secure image can still run with excessive privileges. Live cluster security requires additional runtime and admission controls.

The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Secret scanning searches supported files and artifacts for values that may represent credentials or sensitive authentication material. Examples include API tokens, passwords, cloud keys, and private keys. A typical filesystem command is trivy fs --scanners secret . Detection results should be handled as confidential security data because reports may reveal sensitive locations or values. If a real credential is exposed, remove the exposure where appropriate, revoke or rotate the credential, investigate possible misuse, and move future secrets into an approved secrets manager.

For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "CI Pipeline Integration — Secret Detection", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "CI Pipeline Integration", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. The engineer should also understand the limitations of the check and know when additional application, infrastructure, or runtime security validation is necessary.

# CI Pipeline Integration — SBOM and Supply Chain Security

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "CI Pipeline Integration — SBOM and Supply Chain Security" within the navigation topic "CI Pipeline Integration" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of SBOM Generation. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

A Software Bill of Materials is an inventory of software components contained in an application or artifact. It supports vulnerability investigations, license review, supply-chain visibility, and impact analysis when a package becomes unsafe. Trivy can generate supported SBOM formats for scanned targets. For example, trivy image --format cyclonedx --output sbom.json my-app:latest generates a CycloneDX output for an accessible image. Associate the SBOM with the exact image digest and release identifier. An SBOM is an inventory, not a guarantee that the listed software is secure.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Pipeline execution: explain where the scan belongs in the delivery workflow, how the target artifact is selected, how exit codes are evaluated, and how reports and failures are handled.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

## 4. Practical DevOps Workflow

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "CI Pipeline Integration — SBOM and Supply Chain Security", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "CI Pipeline Integration", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. The engineer should also understand the limitations of the check and know when additional application, infrastructure, or runtime security validation is necessary.

# CI Pipeline Integration — Policy and Exception Management

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "CI Pipeline Integration — Policy and Exception Management" within the navigation topic "CI Pipeline Integration" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Ignore Policies. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Ignore policies determine how selected findings are treated during reporting or automated enforcement. They may be needed for verified false positives, accepted risks, or findings awaiting a controlled remediation. An exception does not remove the underlying vulnerability or make the affected artifact secure. Use the narrowest supported scope, document the finding identifier and reason, assign an accountable owner, obtain approval, and review exceptions periodically. Validate the ignore configuration against the installed Trivy version and confirm that unrelated findings remain visible.

# CI Pipeline Integration — Production Security Workflow

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "CI Pipeline Integration — Production Security Workflow" within the navigation topic "CI Pipeline Integration" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Severity Classification. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Severity classification communicates the assessed seriousness of a security finding. Trivy reports severity values such as UNKNOWN, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, and CRITICAL where supported by the underlying vulnerability information. Severity is an important prioritization signal, but it is not a complete measure of business risk. Exploitability, exposure, affected runtime paths, compensating controls, and asset importance also matter. A production policy should define thresholds, ownership, escalation, and exception approval rather than treating every finding with the same operational response.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Severity interpretation: explain how severity is represented, how teams should interpret the rating, why severity is not identical to exploitability, and how risk-based policy should be applied.

# Vulnerability Remediation — Security Scanning Fundamentals

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Vulnerability Remediation — Security Scanning Fundamentals" within the navigation topic "Vulnerability Remediation" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Vulnerability Remediation. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Vulnerability remediation removes or reduces the risk represented by a security finding. Begin by confirming the affected package, installed version, advisory identifier, and available fixed version. Determine whether the package is direct or transitive and identify the dependency or base image responsible. Update the appropriate dependency or rebuild from a patched base image, run automated tests, rebuild the final artifact, and scan it again. Do not close a finding merely because a source manifest changed; verify that the released image contains the corrected package version.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Remediation: explain how to identify the affected component, select a supported fixed version, evaluate compatibility, test the change, rebuild the artifact, and verify the result with a fresh scan.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "Vulnerability Remediation — Security Scanning Fundamentals", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "Vulnerability Remediation", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. The engineer should also understand the limitations of the check and know when additional application, infrastructure, or runtime security validation is necessary.

# Vulnerability Remediation — Scanner Installation and Configuration

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Vulnerability Remediation — Scanner Installation and Configuration" within the navigation topic "Vulnerability Remediation" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Vulnerability Remediation. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Vulnerability remediation removes or reduces the risk represented by a security finding. Begin by confirming the affected package, installed version, advisory identifier, and available fixed version. Determine whether the package is direct or transitive and identify the dependency or base image responsible. Update the appropriate dependency or rebuild from a patched base image, run automated tests, rebuild the final artifact, and scan it again. Do not close a finding merely because a source manifest changed; verify that the released image contains the corrected package version.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Installation and setup: explain the required executable, supported environment, version verification, configuration, permissions, and network or database prerequisites.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

## 4. Practical DevOps Workflow

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "Vulnerability Remediation — Scanner Installation and Configuration", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "Vulnerability Remediation", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. The engineer should also understand the limitations of the check and know when additional application, infrastructure, or runtime security validation is necessary.

# Vulnerability Remediation — Severity and Risk Evaluation

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Vulnerability Remediation — Severity and Risk Evaluation" within the navigation topic "Vulnerability Remediation" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Severity Classification. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Severity classification communicates the assessed seriousness of a security finding. Trivy reports severity values such as UNKNOWN, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, and CRITICAL where supported by the underlying vulnerability information. Severity is an important prioritization signal, but it is not a complete measure of business risk. Exploitability, exposure, affected runtime paths, compensating controls, and asset importance also matter. A production policy should define thresholds, ownership, escalation, and exception approval rather than treating every finding with the same operational response.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Severity interpretation: explain how severity is represented, how teams should interpret the rating, why severity is not identical to exploitability, and how risk-based policy should be applied.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Kubernetes configuration scanning examines supported manifests and deployment definitions for security weaknesses. Important areas include container privilege settings, host namespace usage, privilege escalation, capabilities, resource exposure, service accounts, and security context configuration. Trivy config can scan supported manifest files, while image scanning separately evaluates the referenced container image. These checks answer different questions: a secure manifest can still reference a vulnerable image, and a secure image can still run with excessive privileges. Live cluster security requires additional runtime and admission controls.

# Vulnerability Remediation — Secret Detection

## 2. Technical Explanation

Secret scanning searches supported files and artifacts for values that may represent credentials or sensitive authentication material. Examples include API tokens, passwords, cloud keys, and private keys. A typical filesystem command is trivy fs --scanners secret . Detection results should be handled as confidential security data because reports may reveal sensitive locations or values. If a real credential is exposed, remove the exposure where appropriate, revoke or rotate the credential, investigate possible misuse, and move future secrets into an approved secrets manager.

# Vulnerability Remediation — SBOM and Supply Chain Security

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Vulnerability Remediation — SBOM and Supply Chain Security" within the navigation topic "Vulnerability Remediation" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

A Software Bill of Materials is an inventory of software components contained in an application or artifact. It supports vulnerability investigations, license review, supply-chain visibility, and impact analysis when a package becomes unsafe. Trivy can generate supported SBOM formats for scanned targets. For example, trivy image --format cyclonedx --output sbom.json my-app:latest generates a CycloneDX output for an accessible image. Associate the SBOM with the exact image digest and release identifier. An SBOM is an inventory, not a guarantee that the listed software is secure.

The engineer should also understand the limitations of the check and know when additional application, infrastructure, or runtime security validation is necessary.

# Vulnerability Remediation — Policy and Exception Management

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Vulnerability Remediation — Policy and Exception Management" within the navigation topic "Vulnerability Remediation" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Ignore Policies. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Ignore policies determine how selected findings are treated during reporting or automated enforcement. They may be needed for verified false positives, accepted risks, or findings awaiting a controlled remediation. An exception does not remove the underlying vulnerability or make the affected artifact secure. Use the narrowest supported scope, document the finding identifier and reason, assign an accountable owner, obtain approval, and review exceptions periodically. Validate the ignore configuration against the installed Trivy version and confirm that unrelated findings remain visible.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Remediation: explain how to identify the affected component, select a supported fixed version, evaluate compatibility, test the change, rebuild the artifact, and verify the result with a fresh scan.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

## 4. Practical DevOps Workflow

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "Vulnerability Remediation — Policy and Exception Management", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "Vulnerability Remediation", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. The engineer should also understand the limitations of the check and know when additional application, infrastructure, or runtime security validation is necessary.

## 2. Technical Explanation

CI pipeline integration runs security checks as part of the automated software delivery process. A practical sequence is source checkout, dependency validation, build, image scan, policy evaluation, artifact publication, and deployment. Trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity HIGH,CRITICAL my-app:latest can be used to make selected findings return a failing exit status. # Vulnerability Remediation — Remediation and Verification

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Vulnerability Remediation — Remediation and Verification" within the navigation topic "Vulnerability Remediation" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Vulnerability Remediation. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Vulnerability remediation removes or reduces the risk represented by a security finding. Begin by confirming the affected package, installed version, advisory identifier, and available fixed version. Determine whether the package is direct or transitive and identify the dependency or base image responsible. Update the appropriate dependency or rebuild from a patched base image, run automated tests, rebuild the final artifact, and scan it again. Do not close a finding merely because a source manifest changed; verify that the released image contains the corrected package version.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Remediation: explain how to identify the affected component, select a supported fixed version, evaluate compatibility, test the change, rebuild the artifact, and verify the result with a fresh scan.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

## 4. Practical DevOps Workflow

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

# Vulnerability Remediation — Production Security Workflow

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Vulnerability Remediation — Production Security Workflow" within the navigation topic "Vulnerability Remediation" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Severity Classification. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Severity classification communicates the assessed seriousness of a security finding. Trivy reports severity values such as UNKNOWN, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, and CRITICAL where supported by the underlying vulnerability information. Severity is an important prioritization signal, but it is not a complete measure of business risk. Exploitability, exposure, affected runtime paths, compensating controls, and asset importance also matter. A production policy should define thresholds, ownership, escalation, and exception approval rather than treating every finding with the same operational response.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Severity interpretation: explain how severity is represented, how teams should interpret the rating, why severity is not identical to exploitability, and how risk-based policy should be applied.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. ## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

# Troubleshooting — Security Scanning Fundamentals

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Troubleshooting — Security Scanning Fundamentals" within the navigation topic "Troubleshooting" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Troubleshooting. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Trivy troubleshooting begins by separating scanner execution problems from actual security findings. Common causes include an incorrect target path, unsupported file formats, registry authentication failures, network or proxy problems, unavailable vulnerability databases, permission errors, and invalid command options. Collect the command, scanner version, target identity, exit status, and relevant error output without exposing secrets. Verify the target independently, check database and registry connectivity, and repeat the scan after correcting the cause. A failed or incomplete scan must never be interpreted as a clean security result.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Troubleshooting: explain the symptoms, likely technical causes, evidence to collect, diagnostic commands, safe corrective actions, and the validation required before closing the issue.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

## 4. Practical DevOps Workflow

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "Troubleshooting — Security Scanning Fundamentals", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "Troubleshooting", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. The engineer should also understand the limitations of the check and know when additional application, infrastructure, or runtime security validation is necessary.

# Troubleshooting — Scanner Installation and Configuration

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Troubleshooting — Scanner Installation and Configuration" within the navigation topic "Troubleshooting" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Troubleshooting. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Trivy troubleshooting begins by separating scanner execution problems from actual security findings. Common causes include an incorrect target path, unsupported file formats, registry authentication failures, network or proxy problems, unavailable vulnerability databases, permission errors, and invalid command options. Collect the command, scanner version, target identity, exit status, and relevant error output without exposing secrets. Verify the target independently, check database and registry connectivity, and repeat the scan after correcting the cause. A failed or incomplete scan must never be interpreted as a clean security result.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Installation and setup: explain the required executable, supported environment, version verification, configuration, permissions, and network or database prerequisites.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

## 4. Practical DevOps Workflow

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. # Troubleshooting — Severity and Risk Evaluation

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Troubleshooting — Severity and Risk Evaluation" within the navigation topic "Troubleshooting" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Severity classification communicates the assessed seriousness of a security finding. Trivy reports severity values such as UNKNOWN, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, and CRITICAL where supported by the underlying vulnerability information. Severity is an important prioritization signal, but it is not a complete measure of business risk. Exploitability, exposure, affected runtime paths, compensating controls, and asset importance also matter. A production policy should define thresholds, ownership, escalation, and exception approval rather than treating every finding with the same operational response.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Kubernetes configuration scanning examines supported manifests and deployment definitions for security weaknesses. Important areas include container privilege settings, host namespace usage, privilege escalation, capabilities, resource exposure, service accounts, and security context configuration. Trivy config can scan supported manifest files, while image scanning separately evaluates the referenced container image. These checks answer different questions: a secure manifest can still reference a vulnerable image, and a secure image can still run with excessive privileges. Live cluster security requires additional runtime and admission controls.

# Troubleshooting — Secret Detection

## 2. Technical Explanation

Secret scanning searches supported files and artifacts for values that may represent credentials or sensitive authentication material. Examples include API tokens, passwords, cloud keys, and private keys. A typical filesystem command is trivy fs --scanners secret . Detection results should be handled as confidential security data because reports may reveal sensitive locations or values. If a real credential is exposed, remove the exposure where appropriate, revoke or rotate the credential, investigate possible misuse, and move future secrets into an approved secrets manager.

# Troubleshooting — SBOM and Supply Chain Security

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Troubleshooting — SBOM and Supply Chain Security" within the navigation topic "Troubleshooting" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of SBOM Generation. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

A Software Bill of Materials is an inventory of software components contained in an application or artifact. It supports vulnerability investigations, license review, supply-chain visibility, and impact analysis when a package becomes unsafe. Trivy can generate supported SBOM formats for scanned targets. For example, trivy image --format cyclonedx --output sbom.json my-app:latest generates a CycloneDX output for an accessible image. Associate the SBOM with the exact image digest and release identifier. An SBOM is an inventory, not a guarantee that the listed software is secure.

Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "Troubleshooting — SBOM and Supply Chain Security", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "Troubleshooting", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. The engineer should also understand the limitations of the check and know when additional application, infrastructure, or runtime security validation is necessary.

# Troubleshooting — Policy and Exception Management

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Troubleshooting — Policy and Exception Management" within the navigation topic "Troubleshooting" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Ignore Policies. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Ignore policies determine how selected findings are treated during reporting or automated enforcement. They may be needed for verified false positives, accepted risks, or findings awaiting a controlled remediation. An exception does not remove the underlying vulnerability or make the affected artifact secure. Use the narrowest supported scope, document the finding identifier and reason, assign an accountable owner, obtain approval, and review exceptions periodically. Validate the ignore configuration against the installed Trivy version and confirm that unrelated findings remain visible.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Troubleshooting: explain the symptoms, likely technical causes, evidence to collect, diagnostic commands, safe corrective actions, and the validation required before closing the issue.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

## 4. Practical DevOps Workflow

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "Troubleshooting — Policy and Exception Management", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "Troubleshooting", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. Do not close a finding merely because a source manifest changed; verify that the released image contains the corrected package version.

# Troubleshooting — Troubleshooting and Diagnostics — Troubleshooting [stage-7-topic-15-section-14]

## 1. Overview and Purpose

## 2. Technical Explanation

Trivy troubleshooting begins by separating scanner execution problems from actual security findings. Common causes include an incorrect target path, unsupported file formats, registry authentication failures, network or proxy problems, unavailable vulnerability databases, permission errors, and invalid command options. Collect the command, scanner version, target identity, exit status, and relevant error output without exposing secrets. Verify the target independently, check database and registry connectivity, and repeat the scan after correcting the cause. A failed or incomplete scan must never be interpreted as a clean security result.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Severity classification communicates the assessed seriousness of a security finding. Trivy reports severity values such as UNKNOWN, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, and CRITICAL where supported by the underlying vulnerability information. Severity is an important prioritization signal, but it is not a complete measure of business risk. Exploitability, exposure, affected runtime paths, compensating controls, and asset importance also matter. A production policy should define thresholds, ownership, escalation, and exception approval rather than treating every finding with the same operational response.

Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "Production Hands-on Lab — Scanner Installation and Configuration", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "Production Hands-on Lab", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. The engineer should also understand the limitations of the check and know when additional application, infrastructure, or runtime security validation is necessary.

# Production Hands-on Lab — Severity and Risk Evaluation

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Production Hands-on Lab — Severity and Risk Evaluation" within the navigation topic "Production Hands-on Lab" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Severity Classification. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Severity classification communicates the assessed seriousness of a security finding. Trivy reports severity values such as UNKNOWN, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, and CRITICAL where supported by the underlying vulnerability information. Severity is an important prioritization signal, but it is not a complete measure of business risk. Exploitability, exposure, affected runtime paths, compensating controls, and asset importance also matter. A production policy should define thresholds, ownership, escalation, and exception approval rather than treating every finding with the same operational response.

## 2. Technical Explanation

A Software Bill of Materials is an inventory of software components contained in an application or artifact. For example, trivy image --format cyclonedx --output sbom.json my-app:latest generates a CycloneDX output for an accessible image. Associate the SBOM with the exact image digest and release identifier. An SBOM is an inventory, not a guarantee that the listed software is secure.

# Production Hands-on Lab — CI Pipeline Integration

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Production Hands-on Lab — CI Pipeline Integration" within the navigation topic "Production Hands-on Lab" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of CI Pipeline Integration. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

CI pipeline integration runs security checks as part of the automated software delivery process. A practical sequence is source checkout, dependency validation, build, image scan, policy evaluation, artifact publication, and deployment. Trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity HIGH,CRITICAL my-app:latest can be used to make selected findings return a failing exit status. The pipeline must distinguish a security-policy failure from a scanner execution failure. Scan the final artifact, use immutable digests, protect report files, and make failure details available to the responsible engineering team.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Pipeline execution: explain where the scan belongs in the delivery workflow, how the target artifact is selected, how exit codes are evaluated, and how reports and failures are handled.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

## 4. Practical DevOps Workflow

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "Production Hands-on Lab — CI Pipeline Integration", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "Production Hands-on Lab", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. The engineer should also understand the limitations of the check and know when additional application, infrastructure, or runtime security validation is necessary.

Determine whether the package is direct or transitive and identify the dependency or base image responsible. Do not close a finding merely because a source manifest changed; verify that the released image contains the corrected package version.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Trivy troubleshooting begins by separating scanner execution problems from actual security findings. Common causes include an incorrect target path, unsupported file formats, registry authentication failures, network or proxy problems, unavailable vulnerability databases, permission errors, and invalid command options. Collect the command, scanner version, target identity, exit status, and relevant error output without exposing secrets. Verify the target independently, check database and registry connectivity, and repeat the scan after correcting the cause. A failed or incomplete scan must never be interpreted as a clean security result.

# Production Hands-on Lab — Production Security Workflow

## 1. Overview and Purpose

The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Severity classification communicates the assessed seriousness of a security finding. Trivy reports severity values such as UNKNOWN, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, and CRITICAL where supported by the underlying vulnerability information. Severity is an important prioritization signal, but it is not a complete measure of business risk. Exploitability, exposure, affected runtime paths, compensating controls, and asset importance also matter. A production policy should define thresholds, ownership, escalation, and exception approval rather than treating every finding with the same operational response.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

## 4. Practical DevOps Workflow

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "Production Hands-on Lab — Container Image Assessment — Production Hands-on Lab [stage-7-topic-16-section-20]", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "Production Hands-on Lab", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. The engineer should also understand the limitations of the check and know when additional application, infrastructure, or runtime security validation is necessary.
