Use short-lived credentials, protect sensitive command output, and separate development and production responsibilities. Record image provenance and verify the exact artifact that is promoted. Do not treat a successful command as sufficient evidence until the resulting AWS resource or image metadata has been checked.

### 5. Troubleshooting and verification

If creation fails, inspect the repository name, Region, caller identity, ECR creation permission, account restrictions, and existing repository state. If a push later fails, verify that the image URI refers to the repository that was actually created.

Verify the outcome by checking the AWS CLI response, repository configuration, image metadata, tag, digest, and relevant CloudTrail activity. When a failure occurs, collect the exact error message, caller identity, requested action, resource ARN, account, Region, and timestamp. Change only the configuration responsible for the failure, then repeat the operation using the same identity and environment.

### 6. DevOps pipeline application

In a CI/CD pipeline, this section should become an explicit and testable pipeline responsibility. The pipeline should validate its prerequisites, use an approved IAM role, execute the required operation, inspect the result, and stop when validation fails. Store the resulting image reference and digest with the build metadata. Pass verified artifact information to the deployment stage so that downstream environments use the intended image rather than an unverified local build.

### 7. Engineering checklist

- Confirm the correct AWS account and Region.
- Confirm the ECR repository and image reference.
- Use the intended IAM identity and least-privilege permissions.
- Verify the operation using AWS metadata or Docker inspection.
- Record the image tag and digest where applicable.
- Check security, retention, and rollback requirements.
- Preserve diagnostic evidence and avoid exposing credentials.

ID: stage-9-topic-4-section-1
HEADING: AWS IAM Permissions — Registry Fundamentals and Architecture
CONTENT LENGTH: 4422
CONTENT:
## AWS IAM Permissions — Registry Fundamentals and Architecture

### 1. Technical explanation

Explain the meaning, purpose, business value, main components, and where this capability fits into a container delivery platform. Clarify the difference between this concept and related ECR concepts so a beginner can understand when and why it is used.

ECR uses AWS IAM to authorize registry operations. IAM identity policies define what an AWS principal can do, while repository policies can grant access to selected principals outside or inside the repository-owning account. Authentication alone does not grant permission to publish or download images.

### 2. How this works in practice

A CI role obtains AWS credentials and requests an ECR authorization token. Publishing requires permissions for checking layers, initiating uploads, uploading parts, completing uploads, and publishing the image manifest. Pulling requires permissions to retrieve image manifests and download layers.

For this section, the engineer should understand the relationship between the selected operation and the complete ECR image lifecycle. Confirm the target AWS account, Region, repository, and image reference before performing an operation. Use the identity intended for the actual pipeline or runtime instead of relying only on an administrator account. Record the relevant resource ARN, image tag, digest, and operation result so the work can be traced later.

### 3. Practical AWS and Docker implementation

The following commands are relevant examples for this topic. Replace ACCOUNT_ID, repository names, image versions, role names, and Regions with values from the actual environment. Review commands before running any operation that changes AWS resources.

aws sts get-caller-identity
aws iam get-role --role-name DevMavoxECRPushRole
aws ecr get-repository-policy --repository-name payments-api --region ap-south-1

### 4. Security and production considerations

Use separate roles for publishing, pulling, and administration. Scope repository actions to the intended repository ARN. Grant only the actions required by the workflow. Evaluate permission boundaries, session policies, and organization service control policies as part of the authorization design.

Production implementation should be repeatable and reviewable. Keep infrastructure configuration and IAM policies in version control. Use short-lived credentials, protect sensitive command output, and separate development and production responsibilities. Record image provenance and verify the exact artifact that is promoted. Do not treat a successful command as sufficient evidence until the resulting AWS resource or image metadata has been checked.

### 5. Troubleshooting and verification

For AccessDenied, identify the exact caller, denied action, resource ARN, and request Region. Inspect identity policies, repository policies, permission boundaries, session policies, service control policies, and KMS permissions where applicable. Avoid fixing a narrow permission problem by granting AdministratorAccess.

Verify the outcome by checking the AWS CLI response, repository configuration, image metadata, tag, digest, and relevant CloudTrail activity. When a failure occurs, collect the exact error message, caller identity, requested action, resource ARN, account, Region, and timestamp. Change only the configuration responsible for the failure, then repeat the operation using the same identity and environment.

### 6. DevOps pipeline application

In a CI/CD pipeline, this section should become an explicit and testable pipeline responsibility. The pipeline should validate its prerequisites, use an approved IAM role, execute the required operation, inspect the result, and stop when validation fails. Store the resulting image reference and digest with the build metadata. Pass verified artifact information to the deployment stage so that downstream environments use the intended image rather than an unverified local build.

### 7. Engineering checklist

- Confirm the correct AWS account and Region.
- Confirm the ECR repository and image reference.
- Use the intended IAM identity and least-privilege permissions.
- Verify the operation using AWS metadata or Docker inspection.
- Record the image tag and digest where applicable.
- Check security, retention, and rollback requirements.
- Preserve diagnostic evidence and avoid exposing credentials.

A CI role obtains AWS credentials and requests an ECR authorization token. Publishing requires permissions for checking layers, initiating uploads, uploading parts, completing uploads, and publishing the image manifest. Pulling requires permissions to retrieve image manifests and download layers.

For this section, the engineer should understand the relationship between the selected operation and the complete ECR image lifecycle. Confirm the target AWS account, Region, repository, and image reference before performing an operation. Use the identity intended for the actual pipeline or runtime instead of relying only on an administrator account. Record the relevant resource ARN, image tag, digest, and operation result so the work can be traced later.

### 3. Practical AWS and Docker implementation

The following commands are relevant examples for this topic. Replace ACCOUNT_ID, repository names, image versions, role names, and Regions with values from the actual environment. Review commands before running any operation that changes AWS resources.

aws sts get-caller-identity
aws iam get-role --role-name DevMavoxECRPushRole
aws ecr get-repository-policy --repository-name payments-api --region ap-south-1

### 4. Security and production considerations

Use separate roles for publishing, pulling, and administration. Scope repository actions to the intended repository ARN. Grant only the actions required by the workflow. Evaluate permission boundaries, session policies, and organization service control policies as part of the authorization design.

Production implementation should be repeatable and reviewable. Keep infrastructure configuration and IAM policies in version control. Use short-lived credentials, protect sensitive command output, and separate development and production responsibilities. Record image provenance and verify the exact artifact that is promoted. Do not treat a successful command as sufficient evidence until the resulting AWS resource or image metadata has been checked.

### 5. Troubleshooting and verification

For AccessDenied, identify the exact caller, denied action, resource ARN, and request Region. Inspect identity policies, repository policies, permission boundaries, session policies, service control policies, and KMS permissions where applicable. Avoid fixing a narrow permission problem by granting AdministratorAccess.

Verify the outcome by checking the AWS CLI response, repository configuration, image metadata, tag, digest, and relevant CloudTrail activity. When a failure occurs, collect the exact error message, caller identity, requested action, resource ARN, account, Region, and timestamp. Change only the configuration responsible for the failure, then repeat the operation using the same identity and environment.

### 6. DevOps pipeline application

In a CI/CD pipeline, this section should become an explicit and testable pipeline responsibility. The pipeline should validate its prerequisites, use an approved IAM role, execute the required operation, inspect the result, and stop when validation fails. Store the resulting image reference and digest with the build metadata. Pass verified artifact information to the deployment stage so that downstream environments use the intended image rather than an unverified local build.

### 7. Engineering checklist

- Confirm the correct AWS account and Region.
- Confirm the ECR repository and image reference.
- Use the intended IAM identity and least-privilege permissions.
- Verify the operation using AWS metadata or Docker inspection.
- Record the image tag and digest where applicable.
- Check security, retention, and rollback requirements.
- Preserve diagnostic evidence and avoid exposing credentials.

Verify the outcome by checking the AWS CLI response, repository configuration, image metadata, tag, digest, and relevant CloudTrail activity. When a failure occurs, collect the exact error message, caller identity, requested action, resource ARN, account, Region, and timestamp. Change only the configuration responsible for the failure, then repeat the operation using the same identity and environment.

### 6. DevOps pipeline application

In a CI/CD pipeline, this section should become an explicit and testable pipeline responsibility. The pipeline should validate its prerequisites, use an approved IAM role, execute the required operation, inspect the result, and stop when validation fails. Store the resulting image reference and digest with the build metadata. Pass verified artifact information to the deployment stage so that downstream environments use the intended image rather than an unverified local build.

### 7. Engineering checklist

- Confirm the correct AWS account and Region.
- Confirm the ECR repository and image reference.
- Use the intended IAM identity and least-privilege permissions.
- Verify the operation using AWS metadata or Docker inspection.
- Record the image tag and digest where applicable.
- Check security, retention, and rollback requirements.

CONTENT:
## AWS IAM Permissions — Registry Fundamentals and Architecture — AWS IAM Permissions [stage-9-topic-4-section-15]

### 1. Technical explanation

Explain the meaning, purpose, business value, main components, and where this capability fits into a container delivery platform. Clarify the difference between this concept and related ECR concepts so a beginner can understand when and why it is used.

ECR uses AWS IAM to authorize registry operations. IAM identity policies define what an AWS principal can do, while repository policies can grant access to selected principals outside or inside the repository-owning account. Authentication alone does not grant permission to publish or download images.

### 2. How this works in practice

A CI role obtains AWS credentials and requests an ECR authorization token. Publishing requires permissions for checking layers, initiating uploads, uploading parts, completing uploads, and publishing the image manifest. Pulling requires permissions to retrieve image manifests and download layers.

For this section, the engineer should understand the relationship between the selected operation and the complete ECR image lifecycle. Confirm the target AWS account, Region, repository, and image reference before performing an operation. Use the identity intended for the actual pipeline or runtime instead of relying only on an administrator account. Record the relevant resource ARN, image tag, digest, and operation result so the work can be traced later.

### 3. Practical AWS and Docker implementation

The following commands are relevant examples for this topic. Replace ACCOUNT_ID, repository names, image versions, role names, and Regions with values from the actual environment. Review commands before running any operation that changes AWS resources.

aws sts get-caller-identity
aws iam get-role --role-name DevMavoxECRPushRole
aws ecr get-repository-policy --repository-name payments-api --region ap-south-1

### 4. Security and production considerations

Use separate roles for publishing, pulling, and administration. Scope repository actions to the intended repository ARN. Grant only the actions required by the workflow. Evaluate permission boundaries, session policies, and organization service control policies as part of the authorization design.

Production implementation should be repeatable and reviewable. Keep infrastructure configuration and IAM policies in version control. Use short-lived credentials, protect sensitive command output, and separate development and production responsibilities. Record image provenance and verify the exact artifact that is promoted. Do not treat a successful command as sufficient evidence until the resulting AWS resource or image metadata has been checked.

### 5. Troubleshooting and verification

For AccessDenied, identify the exact caller, denied action, resource ARN, and request Region. Inspect identity policies, repository policies, permission boundaries, session policies, service control policies, and KMS permissions where applicable. Avoid fixing a narrow permission problem by granting AdministratorAccess.

ID: stage-9-topic-5-section-1
HEADING: Docker Authentication — Registry Fundamentals and Architecture
CONTENT LENGTH: 4263
CONTENT:
## Docker Authentication — Registry Fundamentals and Architecture

### 1. Technical explanation

Explain the meaning, purpose, business value, main components, and where this capability fits into a container delivery platform. Clarify the difference between this concept and related ECR concepts so a beginner can understand when and why it is used.

Docker authentication establishes a login session between the Docker client and a private ECR registry. The AWS CLI obtains an authorization token for the selected Region. Docker uses the token to authenticate requests to the registry endpoint.

### 2. How this works in practice

Retrieve the ECR password with aws ecr get-login-password and pipe it to docker login using username AWS and password-stdin. The registry hostname must match the target account and Region. Authenticate again when the token expires or when the workflow uses a different registry.

For this section, the engineer should understand the relationship between the selected operation and the complete ECR image lifecycle. Confirm the target AWS account, Region, repository, and image reference before performing an operation. Use the identity intended for the actual pipeline or runtime instead of relying only on an administrator account. Record the relevant resource ARN, image tag, digest, and operation result so the work can be traced later.

### 3. Practical AWS and Docker implementation

The following commands are relevant examples for this topic. Replace ACCOUNT_ID, repository names, image versions, role names, and Regions with values from the actual environment. Review commands before running any operation that changes AWS resources.

aws sts get-caller-identity
aws ecr get-login-password --region ap-south-1 | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com
docker info

### 4. Security and production considerations

Never print the token or place it directly in command-line arguments. Use password-stdin and short-lived AWS credentials. In CI, obtain credentials through an approved role or federation mechanism. Do not save credentials in source control or bake them into an image.

Production implementation should be repeatable and reviewable. Keep infrastructure configuration and IAM policies in version control. Use short-lived credentials, protect sensitive command output, and separate development and production responsibilities. Record image provenance and verify the exact artifact that is promoted. Do not treat a successful command as sufficient evidence until the resulting AWS resource or image metadata has been checked.

### 5. Troubleshooting and verification

Check AWS credential validity, caller identity, token retrieval, Region, registry hostname, Docker credential configuration, proxy settings, and network connectivity. If login succeeds but push fails, investigate repository permissions separately.

Verify the outcome by checking the AWS CLI response, repository configuration, image metadata, tag, digest, and relevant CloudTrail activity. When a failure occurs, collect the exact error message, caller identity, requested action, resource ARN, account, Region, and timestamp. Change only the configuration responsible for the failure, then repeat the operation using the same identity and environment.

### 6. DevOps pipeline application

In a CI/CD pipeline, this section should become an explicit and testable pipeline responsibility. The pipeline should validate its prerequisites, use an approved IAM role, execute the required operation, inspect the result, and stop when validation fails. Store the resulting image reference and digest with the build metadata. Pass verified artifact information to the deployment stage so that downstream environments use the intended image rather than an unverified local build.

### 7. Engineering checklist

- Confirm the correct AWS account and Region.
- Confirm the ECR repository and image reference.
- Use the intended IAM identity and least-privilege permissions.
- Verify the operation using AWS metadata or Docker inspection.
- Record the image tag and digest where applicable.
- Check security, retention, and rollback requirements.
- Preserve diagnostic evidence and avoid exposing credentials.

### 1. Technical explanation

Explain the sequence of operations from the initiating client to the AWS service and the resulting registry state. Describe the components involved, the information exchanged, the dependencies between steps, and what should happen when an individual step fails.

Docker authentication establishes a login session between the Docker client and a private ECR registry. The AWS CLI obtains an authorization token for the selected Region. Docker uses the token to authenticate requests to the registry endpoint.

### 2. How this works in practice

Retrieve the ECR password with aws ecr get-login-password and pipe it to docker login using username AWS and password-stdin. The registry hostname must match the target account and Region. Authenticate again when the token expires or when the workflow uses a different registry.

For this section, the engineer should understand the relationship between the selected operation and the complete ECR image lifecycle. Confirm the target AWS account, Region, repository, and image reference before performing an operation. Use the identity intended for the actual pipeline or runtime instead of relying only on an administrator account. Record the relevant resource ARN, image tag, digest, and operation result so the work can be traced later.

### 3. Practical AWS and Docker implementation

The following commands are relevant examples for this topic. Replace ACCOUNT_ID, repository names, image versions, role names, and Regions with values from the actual environment. Review commands before running any operation that changes AWS resources.

aws sts get-caller-identity
aws ecr get-login-password --region ap-south-1 | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com
docker info

### 4. Security and production considerations

Never print the token or place it directly in command-line arguments. Use password-stdin and short-lived AWS credentials. In CI, obtain credentials through an approved role or federation mechanism. Do not save credentials in source control or bake them into an image.

Production implementation should be repeatable and reviewable. Keep infrastructure configuration and IAM policies in version control. Use short-lived credentials, protect sensitive command output, and separate development and production responsibilities. Record image provenance and verify the exact artifact that is promoted. Do not treat a successful command as sufficient evidence until the resulting AWS resource or image metadata has been checked.

### 5. Troubleshooting and verification

Check AWS credential validity, caller identity, token retrieval, Region, registry hostname, Docker credential configuration, proxy settings, and network connectivity. If login succeeds but push fails, investigate repository permissions separately.

Verify the outcome by checking the AWS CLI response, repository configuration, image metadata, tag, digest, and relevant CloudTrail activity. When a failure occurs, collect the exact error message, caller identity, requested action, resource ARN, account, Region, and timestamp. Change only the configuration responsible for the failure, then repeat the operation using the same identity and environment.

### 6. DevOps pipeline application

In a CI/CD pipeline, this section should become an explicit and testable pipeline responsibility. The pipeline should validate its prerequisites, use an approved IAM role, execute the required operation, inspect the result, and stop when validation fails. Store the resulting image reference and digest with the build metadata. Pass verified artifact information to the deployment stage so that downstream environments use the intended image rather than an unverified local build.

### 7. Engineering checklist

- Confirm the correct AWS account and Region.
- Confirm the ECR repository and image reference.
- Use the intended IAM identity and least-privilege permissions.
- Verify the operation using AWS metadata or Docker inspection.
- Record the image tag and digest where applicable.
- Check security, retention, and rollback requirements.
- Preserve diagnostic evidence and avoid exposing credentials.

Store the resulting image reference and digest with the build metadata. Pass verified artifact information to the deployment stage so that downstream environments use the intended image rather than an unverified local build.

### 7. Engineering checklist

- Confirm the correct AWS account and Region.
- Confirm the ECR repository and image reference.
- Use the intended IAM identity and least-privilege permissions.
- Verify the operation using AWS metadata or Docker inspection.
- Record the image tag and digest where applicable.
- Check security, retention, and rollback requirements.
- Preserve diagnostic evidence and avoid exposing credentials.

CONTENT:
## Image Tagging — Registry Fundamentals and Architecture

### 1. Technical explanation

Explain the meaning, purpose, business value, main components, and where this capability fits into a container delivery platform. Clarify the difference between this concept and related ECR concepts so a beginner can understand when and why it is used.

An image tag is a human-readable reference associated with an image manifest. Teams use release versions, build identifiers, Git commit hashes, and environment-specific labels to identify artifacts. A tag helps people select an image, but it is not necessarily a permanent identity.

### 2. How this works in practice

Build the image, assign a meaningful local tag, and apply the complete ECR repository URI with the intended release tag. Push the ECR reference and verify that the tag appears in repository metadata. Record the digest returned by ECR.

For this section, the engineer should understand the relationship between the selected operation and the complete ECR image lifecycle. Confirm the target AWS account, Region, repository, and image reference before performing an operation. Use the identity intended for the actual pipeline or runtime instead of relying only on an administrator account. Record the relevant resource ARN, image tag, digest, and operation result so the work can be traced later.

### 3. Practical AWS and Docker implementation

The following commands are relevant examples for this topic. Replace ACCOUNT_ID, repository names, image versions, role names, and Regions with values from the actual environment. Review commands before running any operation that changes AWS resources.

docker image ls
docker tag payments-api:1.4.2 ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/payments-api:1.4.2
aws ecr describe-images --repository-name payments-api --region ap-south-1

### 4. Security and production considerations

Use unique release tags and avoid depending on mutable latest references for production. Define a naming convention that connects an image to its source revision and build. Enable immutable tags where overwriting a release would be unsafe.

Production implementation should be repeatable and reviewable. Keep infrastructure configuration and IAM policies in version control. Use short-lived credentials, protect sensitive command output, and separate development and production responsibilities. Record image provenance and verify the exact artifact that is promoted. Do not treat a successful command as sufficient evidence until the resulting AWS resource or image metadata has been checked.

### 5. Troubleshooting and verification

Check spelling, repository URI, tag format, account, Region, local image existence, and repository mutability. If an immutable tag already exists, publish a new unique version rather than attempting to overwrite the existing release.

Verify the outcome by checking the AWS CLI response, repository configuration, image metadata, tag, digest, and relevant CloudTrail activity. When a failure occurs, collect the exact error message, caller identity, requested action, resource ARN, account, Region, and timestamp. Change only the configuration responsible for the failure, then repeat the operation using the same identity and environment.

### 6. DevOps pipeline application

In a CI/CD pipeline, this section should become an explicit and testable pipeline responsibility. The pipeline should validate its prerequisites, use an approved IAM role, execute the required operation, inspect the result, and stop when validation fails. Production implementation should be repeatable and reviewable. Keep infrastructure configuration and IAM policies in version control. Use short-lived credentials, protect sensitive command output, and separate development and production responsibilities. Record image provenance and verify the exact artifact that is promoted. Do not treat a successful command as sufficient evidence until the resulting AWS resource or image metadata has been checked.

### 5. Troubleshooting and verification

Check spelling, repository URI, tag format, account, Region, local image existence, and repository mutability. If an immutable tag already exists, publish a new unique version rather than attempting to overwrite the existing release.

Verify the outcome by checking the AWS CLI response, repository configuration, image metadata, tag, digest, and relevant CloudTrail activity. When a failure occurs, collect the exact error message, caller identity, requested action, resource ARN, account, Region, and timestamp. Change only the configuration responsible for the failure, then repeat the operation using the same identity and environment.

### 6. DevOps pipeline application

In a CI/CD pipeline, this section should become an explicit and testable pipeline responsibility. The pipeline should validate its prerequisites, use an approved IAM role, execute the required operation, inspect the result, and stop when validation fails. Store the resulting image reference and digest with the build metadata. Pass verified artifact information to the deployment stage so that downstream environments use the intended image rather than an unverified local build.

### 7. Engineering checklist

- Confirm the correct AWS account and Region.
- Confirm the ECR repository and image reference.
- Use the intended IAM identity and least-privilege permissions.
- Verify the operation using AWS metadata or Docker inspection.
- Record the image tag and digest where applicable.
- Check security, retention, and rollback requirements.
- Preserve diagnostic evidence and avoid exposing credentials.

ID: stage-9-topic-7-section-1
HEADING: Image Push Workflow — Registry Fundamentals and Architecture
CONTENT LENGTH: 4495
CONTENT:
## Image Push Workflow — Registry Fundamentals and Architecture

### 1. Technical explanation

Explain the meaning, purpose, business value, main components, and where this capability fits into a container delivery platform. Clarify the difference between this concept and related ECR concepts so a beginner can understand when and why it is used.

The ECR push workflow publishes a locally built container image to a private repository. Docker transfers the image manifest and any required layers that are not already available in the registry. ECR validates the caller's permissions before accepting the publication.

### 2. How this works in practice

Build from a known source revision, assign a unique tag, authenticate to the correct registry, tag the image with the complete repository URI, and execute docker push. After the push, query ECR to confirm the tag and capture the image digest.

For this section, the engineer should understand the relationship between the selected operation and the complete ECR image lifecycle. Confirm the target AWS account, Region, repository, and image reference before performing an operation. Use the identity intended for the actual pipeline or runtime instead of relying only on an administrator account. Record the relevant resource ARN, image tag, digest, and operation result so the work can be traced later.

### 3. Practical AWS and Docker implementation

The following commands are relevant examples for this topic. Replace ACCOUNT_ID, repository names, image versions, role names, and Regions with values from the actual environment. Review commands before running any operation that changes AWS resources.

docker build -t payments-api:1.4.2 .
aws ecr get-login-password --region ap-south-1 | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com
docker tag payments-api:1.4.2 ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/payments-api:1.4.2
docker push ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/payments-api:1.4.2
aws ecr describe-images --repository-name payments-api --region ap-south-1

### 4. Security and production considerations

Use a dedicated CI role with narrowly scoped upload permissions. Do not publish unreviewed builds to production repositories. Scan images and enforce release policies before promotion. Preserve build logs and artifact metadata without exposing credentials.

Production implementation should be repeatable and reviewable. Keep infrastructure configuration and IAM policies in version control. Use short-lived credentials, protect sensitive command output, and separate development and production responsibilities. Record image provenance and verify the exact artifact that is promoted. Do not treat a successful command as sufficient evidence until the resulting AWS resource or image metadata has been checked.

### 5. Troubleshooting and verification

Investigate authentication, repository existence, IAM upload actions, network interruptions, tag immutability, image size, and Docker daemon errors. A successful build is not evidence of a successful registry push. Verify the remote image after every publication.

Verify the outcome by checking the AWS CLI response, repository configuration, image metadata, tag, digest, and relevant CloudTrail activity. When a failure occurs, collect the exact error message, caller identity, requested action, resource ARN, account, Region, and timestamp. Change only the configuration responsible for the failure, then repeat the operation using the same identity and environment.

### 6. DevOps pipeline application

In a CI/CD pipeline, this section should become an explicit and testable pipeline responsibility. The pipeline should validate its prerequisites, use an approved IAM role, execute the required operation, inspect the result, and stop when validation fails. Store the resulting image reference and digest with the build metadata. Pass verified artifact information to the deployment stage so that downstream environments use the intended image rather than an unverified local build.

### 7. Engineering checklist

- Confirm the correct AWS account and Region.
- Confirm the ECR repository and image reference.
- Use the intended IAM identity and least-privilege permissions.
- Verify the operation using AWS metadata or Docker inspection.
- Record the image tag and digest where applicable.
- Check security, retention, and rollback requirements.
- Preserve diagnostic evidence and avoid exposing credentials.

When a failure occurs, collect the exact error message, caller identity, requested action, resource ARN, account, Region, and timestamp. Change only the configuration responsible for the failure, then repeat the operation using the same identity and environment.

### 6. DevOps pipeline application

In a CI/CD pipeline, this section should become an explicit and testable pipeline responsibility. The pipeline should validate its prerequisites, use an approved IAM role, execute the required operation, inspect the result, and stop when validation fails. Store the resulting image reference and digest with the build metadata. Pass verified artifact information to the deployment stage so that downstream environments use the intended image rather than an unverified local build.

### 7. Engineering checklist

- Confirm the correct AWS account and Region.
- Confirm the ECR repository and image reference.
- Use the intended IAM identity and least-privilege permissions.
- Verify the operation using AWS metadata or Docker inspection.
- Record the image tag and digest where applicable.
- Check security, retention, and rollback requirements.
- Preserve diagnostic evidence and avoid exposing credentials.

ID: stage-9-topic-7-section-6
HEADING: Image Push Workflow — Image Immutability
CONTENT LENGTH: 4484
CONTENT:
## Image Push Workflow — Image Immutability

### 1. Technical explanation

Explain the sequence of operations from the initiating client to the AWS service and the resulting registry state. Describe the components involved, the information exchanged, the dependencies between steps, and what should happen when an individual step fails.

The ECR push workflow publishes a locally built container image to a private repository. Docker transfers the image manifest and any required layers that are not already available in the registry. ECR validates the caller's permissions before accepting the publication.

### 2. How this works in practice

Build from a known source revision, assign a unique tag, authenticate to the correct registry, tag the image with the complete repository URI, and execute docker push. After the push, query ECR to confirm the tag and capture the image digest.

For this section, the engineer should understand the relationship between the selected operation and the complete ECR image lifecycle. Confirm the target AWS account, Region, repository, and image reference before performing an operation. Use the identity intended for the actual pipeline or runtime instead of relying only on an administrator account. Record the relevant resource ARN, image tag, digest, and operation result so the work can be traced later.

### 3. Practical AWS and Docker implementation

The following commands are relevant examples for this topic. Replace ACCOUNT_ID, repository names, image versions, role names, and Regions with values from the actual environment. Review commands before running any operation that changes AWS resources.

docker build -t payments-api:1.4.2 .
aws ecr get-login-password --region ap-south-1 | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com
docker tag payments-api:1.4.2 ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/payments-api:1.4.2
docker push ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/payments-api:1.4.2
aws ecr describe-images --repository-name payments-api --region ap-south-1

### 4. Security and production considerations

Use a dedicated CI role with narrowly scoped upload permissions. Do not publish unreviewed builds to production repositories. Scan images and enforce release policies before promotion. Preserve build logs and artifact metadata without exposing credentials.

Production implementation should be repeatable and reviewable. Keep infrastructure configuration and IAM policies in version control. Use short-lived credentials, protect sensitive command output, and separate development and production responsibilities. Record image provenance and verify the exact artifact that is promoted. Do not treat a successful command as sufficient evidence until the resulting AWS resource or image metadata has been checked.

### 5. Troubleshooting and verification

Investigate authentication, repository existence, IAM upload actions, network interruptions, tag immutability, image size, and Docker daemon errors. A successful build is not evidence of a successful registry push. Verify the remote image after every publication.

Verify the outcome by checking the AWS CLI response, repository configuration, image metadata, tag, digest, and relevant CloudTrail activity. Use short-lived credentials, protect sensitive command output, and separate development and production responsibilities. Record image provenance and verify the exact artifact that is promoted. Do not treat a successful command as sufficient evidence until the resulting AWS resource or image metadata has been checked.

### 5. Troubleshooting and verification

Investigate authentication, repository existence, IAM upload actions, network interruptions, tag immutability, image size, and Docker daemon errors. A successful build is not evidence of a successful registry push. Verify the remote image after every publication.

Verify the outcome by checking the AWS CLI response, repository configuration, image metadata, tag, digest, and relevant CloudTrail activity. When a failure occurs, collect the exact error message, caller identity, requested action, resource ARN, account, Region, and timestamp. Change only the configuration responsible for the failure, then repeat the operation using the same identity and environment.

### 6. DevOps pipeline application

In a CI/CD pipeline, this section should become an explicit and testable pipeline responsibility. The pipeline should validate its prerequisites, use an approved IAM role, execute the required operation, inspect the result, and stop when validation fails. Store the resulting image reference and digest with the build metadata. Pass verified artifact information to the deployment stage so that downstream environments use the intended image rather than an unverified local build.

### 7. Engineering checklist

- Confirm the correct AWS account and Region.
- Confirm the ECR repository and image reference.
- Use the intended IAM identity and least-privilege permissions.
- Verify the operation using AWS metadata or Docker inspection.
- Record the image tag and digest where applicable.
- Check security, retention, and rollback requirements.
- Preserve diagnostic evidence and avoid exposing credentials.

HEADING: Image Push Workflow — Hands-on Registry Exercise
CONTENT LENGTH: 4492
CONTENT:
## Image Push Workflow — Hands-on Registry Exercise

### 1. Technical explanation

Explain the sequence of operations from the initiating client to the AWS service and the resulting registry state. Describe the components involved, the information exchanged, the dependencies between steps, and what should happen when an individual step fails.

The ECR push workflow publishes a locally built container image to a private repository. Docker transfers the image manifest and any required layers that are not already available in the registry. ECR validates the caller's permissions before accepting the publication.

### 2. How this works in practice

Build from a known source revision, assign a unique tag, authenticate to the correct registry, tag the image with the complete repository URI, and execute docker push. After the push, query ECR to confirm the tag and capture the image digest.

For this section, the engineer should understand the relationship between the selected operation and the complete ECR image lifecycle. Confirm the target AWS account, Region, repository, and image reference before performing an operation. Use the identity intended for the actual pipeline or runtime instead of relying only on an administrator account. Record the relevant resource ARN, image tag, digest, and operation result so the work can be traced later.

### 3. Practical AWS and Docker implementation

The following commands are relevant examples for this topic. Replace ACCOUNT_ID, repository names, image versions, role names, and Regions with values from the actual environment. Review commands before running any operation that changes AWS resources.

docker build -t payments-api:1.4.2 .
aws ecr get-login-password --region ap-south-1 | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com
docker tag payments-api:1.4.2 ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/payments-api:1.4.2
docker push ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/payments-api:1.4.2
aws ecr describe-images --repository-name payments-api --region ap-south-1

### 4. Security and production considerations

Use a dedicated CI role with narrowly scoped upload permissions. Do not publish unreviewed builds to production repositories. Scan images and enforce release policies before promotion. Preserve build logs and artifact metadata without exposing credentials.

ID: stage-9-topic-8-section-1
HEADING: Image Pull Workflow — Registry Fundamentals and Architecture
CONTENT LENGTH: 4397
CONTENT:
## Image Pull Workflow — Registry Fundamentals and Architecture

### 1. Technical explanation

Explain the meaning, purpose, business value, main components, and where this capability fits into a container delivery platform. Clarify the difference between this concept and related ECR concepts so a beginner can understand when and why it is used.

The ECR pull workflow retrieves a container image from a repository into a Docker client or container runtime. The client resolves the image reference, requests the manifest, and downloads the layers needed to construct the image locally.

### 2. How this works in practice

Confirm the target account, Region, repository, and image reference. Authenticate using the identity configured for the environment, then pull the full repository URI and selected tag or digest. In ECS and EKS, ensure the configured execution role or node identity can retrieve the image.

For this section, the engineer should understand the relationship between the selected operation and the complete ECR image lifecycle. Confirm the target AWS account, Region, repository, and image reference before performing an operation. Use the identity intended for the actual pipeline or runtime instead of relying only on an administrator account. Record the relevant resource ARN, image tag, digest, and operation result so the work can be traced later.

### 3. Practical AWS and Docker implementation

The following commands are relevant examples for this topic. Replace ACCOUNT_ID, repository names, image versions, role names, and Regions with values from the actual environment. Review commands before running any operation that changes AWS resources.

aws ecr get-login-password --region ap-south-1 | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com
docker pull ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/payments-api:1.4.2
docker image inspect ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/payments-api:1.4.2

### 4. Security and production considerations

Grant pull permissions only to identities that require the artifact. Use digest references for controlled production deployments. Ensure network access to the registry and required service endpoints. Do not embed registry credentials in container images.

Production implementation should be repeatable and reviewable. Keep infrastructure configuration and IAM policies in version control. Use short-lived credentials, protect sensitive command output, and separate development and production responsibilities. Record image provenance and verify the exact artifact that is promoted. Do not treat a successful command as sufficient evidence until the resulting AWS resource or image metadata has been checked.

### 5. Troubleshooting and verification

For image-pull errors, inspect the exact image URI, repository, tag, digest, authentication token, IAM permissions, network route, DNS, proxy, and runtime identity. Separate image retrieval problems from container startup, application configuration, and readiness failures.

Verify the outcome by checking the AWS CLI response, repository configuration, image metadata, tag, digest, and relevant CloudTrail activity. When a failure occurs, collect the exact error message, caller identity, requested action, resource ARN, account, Region, and timestamp. Change only the configuration responsible for the failure, then repeat the operation using the same identity and environment.

### 6. DevOps pipeline application

In a CI/CD pipeline, this section should become an explicit and testable pipeline responsibility. The pipeline should validate its prerequisites, use an approved IAM role, execute the required operation, inspect the result, and stop when validation fails. Store the resulting image reference and digest with the build metadata. Pass verified artifact information to the deployment stage so that downstream environments use the intended image rather than an unverified local build.

### 7. Engineering checklist

- Confirm the correct AWS account and Region.
- Confirm the ECR repository and image reference.
- Use the intended IAM identity and least-privilege permissions.
- Verify the operation using AWS metadata or Docker inspection.
- Record the image tag and digest where applicable.
- Check security, retention, and rollback requirements.
- Preserve diagnostic evidence and avoid exposing credentials.

For image-pull errors, inspect the exact image URI, repository, tag, digest, authentication token, IAM permissions, network route, DNS, proxy, and runtime identity. Separate image retrieval problems from container startup, application configuration, and readiness failures.

Verify the outcome by checking the AWS CLI response, repository configuration, image metadata, tag, digest, and relevant CloudTrail activity. When a failure occurs, collect the exact error message, caller identity, requested action, resource ARN, account, Region, and timestamp. Change only the configuration responsible for the failure, then repeat the operation using the same identity and environment.

### 6. DevOps pipeline application

In a CI/CD pipeline, this section should become an explicit and testable pipeline responsibility. The pipeline should validate its prerequisites, use an approved IAM role, execute the required operation, inspect the result, and stop when validation fails. Store the resulting image reference and digest with the build metadata. Pass verified artifact information to the deployment stage so that downstream environments use the intended image rather than an unverified local build.

### 7. Engineering checklist

- Confirm the correct AWS account and Region.
- Confirm the ECR repository and image reference.
- Use the intended IAM identity and least-privilege permissions.
- Verify the operation using AWS metadata or Docker inspection.
- Record the image tag and digest where applicable.
- Check security, retention, and rollback requirements.
- Preserve diagnostic evidence and avoid exposing credentials.

HEADING: Image Pull Workflow — Lifecycle and Retention Policies
CONTENT LENGTH: 4400
CONTENT:
## Image Pull Workflow — Lifecycle and Retention Policies

### 1. Technical explanation

Explain the sequence of operations from the initiating client to the AWS service and the resulting registry state. Describe the components involved, the information exchanged, the dependencies between steps, and what should happen when an individual step fails.

The ECR pull workflow retrieves a container image from a repository into a Docker client or container runtime. The client resolves the image reference, requests the manifest, and downloads the layers needed to construct the image locally.

### 2. How this works in practice

Confirm the target account, Region, repository, and image reference. Authenticate using the identity configured for the environment, then pull the full repository URI and selected tag or digest. In ECS and EKS, ensure the configured execution role or node identity can retrieve the image.

For this section, the engineer should understand the relationship between the selected operation and the complete ECR image lifecycle. Confirm the target AWS account, Region, repository, and image reference before performing an operation. Use the identity intended for the actual pipeline or runtime instead of relying only on an administrator account. Record the relevant resource ARN, image tag, digest, and operation result so the work can be traced later.

### 3. Practical AWS and Docker implementation

The following commands are relevant examples for this topic. Replace ACCOUNT_ID, repository names, image versions, role names, and Regions with values from the actual environment. Review commands before running any operation that changes AWS resources.

aws ecr get-login-password --region ap-south-1 | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com
docker pull ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/payments-api:1.4.2
docker image inspect ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/payments-api:1.4.2

### 4. Security and production considerations

Grant pull permissions only to identities that require the artifact. Use digest references for controlled production deployments. Ensure network access to the registry and required service endpoints. Do not embed registry credentials in container images.

Production implementation should be repeatable and reviewable. Keep infrastructure configuration and IAM policies in version control. Use short-lived credentials, protect sensitive command output, and separate development and production responsibilities. Record image provenance and verify the exact artifact that is promoted. Do not treat a successful command as sufficient evidence until the resulting AWS resource or image metadata has been checked.

### 5. Troubleshooting and verification

For image-pull errors, inspect the exact image URI, repository, tag, digest, authentication token, IAM permissions, network route, DNS, proxy, and runtime identity. Separate image retrieval problems from container startup, application configuration, and readiness failures.

ID: stage-9-topic-9-section-1
HEADING: Immutable Image Tags — Registry Fundamentals and Architecture
CONTENT LENGTH: 4303
CONTENT:
## Immutable Image Tags — Registry Fundamentals and Architecture

### 1. Technical explanation

Explain the meaning, purpose, business value, main components, and where this capability fits into a container delivery platform. Clarify the difference between this concept and related ECR concepts so a beginner can understand when and why it is used.

ECR tag immutability prevents an existing image tag from being overwritten by a later push. It protects release references from silently changing to different image content and helps preserve traceability between a deployment and its original artifact.

### 2. How this works in practice

Enable immutable tag settings on the repository, publish each build with a unique release or commit identifier, and verify the image metadata after publication. When a tag already exists, create a new release identifier rather than reusing the protected tag.

For this section, the engineer should understand the relationship between the selected operation and the complete ECR image lifecycle. Confirm the target AWS account, Region, repository, and image reference before performing an operation. Use the identity intended for the actual pipeline or runtime instead of relying only on an administrator account. Record the relevant resource ARN, image tag, digest, and operation result so the work can be traced later.

### 3. Practical AWS and Docker implementation

The following commands are relevant examples for this topic. Replace ACCOUNT_ID, repository names, image versions, role names, and Regions with values from the actual environment. Review commands before running any operation that changes AWS resources.

aws ecr describe-repositories --repository-names payments-api --region ap-south-1
aws ecr put-image-tag-mutability --repository-name payments-api --image-tag-mutability IMMUTABLE --region ap-south-1
aws ecr describe-images --repository-name payments-api --region ap-south-1

### 4. Security and production considerations

Use immutable tags for approved release artifacts and combine them with digest pinning, image scanning, and controlled promotion. Document any permitted exclusions or mutable-tag workflows. Limit repository configuration changes to authorized administrators.

Production implementation should be repeatable and reviewable. Keep infrastructure configuration and IAM policies in version control. Use short-lived credentials, protect sensitive command output, and separate development and production responsibilities. Record image provenance and verify the exact artifact that is promoted. Do not treat a successful command as sufficient evidence until the resulting AWS resource or image metadata has been checked.

### 5. Troubleshooting and verification

A push rejected because a tag already exists may indicate that immutability is working as designed. Check repository settings and the existing image digest. Do not delete an approved image simply to reuse its tag.

Verify the outcome by checking the AWS CLI response, repository configuration, image metadata, tag, digest, and relevant CloudTrail activity. When a failure occurs, collect the exact error message, caller identity, requested action, resource ARN, account, Region, and timestamp. Change only the configuration responsible for the failure, then repeat the operation using the same identity and environment.

### 6. DevOps pipeline application

In a CI/CD pipeline, this section should become an explicit and testable pipeline responsibility. The pipeline should validate its prerequisites, use an approved IAM role, execute the required operation, inspect the result, and stop when validation fails. Store the resulting image reference and digest with the build metadata. Pass verified artifact information to the deployment stage so that downstream environments use the intended image rather than an unverified local build.

### 7. Engineering checklist

- Confirm the correct AWS account and Region.
- Confirm the ECR repository and image reference.
- Use the intended IAM identity and least-privilege permissions.
- Verify the operation using AWS metadata or Docker inspection.
- Record the image tag and digest where applicable.
- Check security, retention, and rollback requirements.
- Preserve diagnostic evidence and avoid exposing credentials.

### 5. Troubleshooting and verification

A push rejected because a tag already exists may indicate that immutability is working as designed. Check repository settings and the existing image digest. Do not delete an approved image simply to reuse its tag.

Verify the outcome by checking the AWS CLI response, repository configuration, image metadata, tag, digest, and relevant CloudTrail activity. When a failure occurs, collect the exact error message, caller identity, requested action, resource ARN, account, Region, and timestamp. Change only the configuration responsible for the failure, then repeat the operation using the same identity and environment.

### 6. DevOps pipeline application

In a CI/CD pipeline, this section should become an explicit and testable pipeline responsibility. The pipeline should validate its prerequisites, use an approved IAM role, execute the required operation, inspect the result, and stop when validation fails. Store the resulting image reference and digest with the build metadata. Pass verified artifact information to the deployment stage so that downstream environments use the intended image rather than an unverified local build.

### 7. Engineering checklist

- Confirm the correct AWS account and Region.
- Confirm the ECR repository and image reference.
- Use the intended IAM identity and least-privilege permissions.
- Verify the operation using AWS metadata or Docker inspection.
- Record the image tag and digest where applicable.
- Check security, retention, and rollback requirements.
- Preserve diagnostic evidence and avoid exposing credentials.

## Immutable Image Tags — Cross-account Integration

### 1. Technical explanation

Explain how the image reference identifies the artifact, how tags and digests differ, how the value is assigned and verified, and how it affects release traceability. Include the risks of mutable references and the value of immutable release identifiers.

ECR tag immutability prevents an existing image tag from being overwritten by a later push. It protects release references from silently changing to different image content and helps preserve traceability between a deployment and its original artifact.

### 2. How this works in practice

Enable immutable tag settings on the repository, publish each build with a unique release or commit identifier, and verify the image metadata after publication. When a tag already exists, create a new release identifier rather than reusing the protected tag.

For this section, the engineer should understand the relationship between the selected operation and the complete ECR image lifecycle. Confirm the target AWS account, Region, repository, and image reference before performing an operation. Use the identity intended for the actual pipeline or runtime instead of relying only on an administrator account. Record the relevant resource ARN, image tag, digest, and operation result so the work can be traced later.

### 4. Security and production considerations

Use immutable tags for approved release artifacts and combine them with digest pinning, image scanning, and controlled promotion. Document any permitted exclusions or mutable-tag workflows. Limit repository configuration changes to authorized administrators.

ID: stage-9-topic-10-section-1
HEADING: Image Digests — Registry Fundamentals and Architecture
CONTENT LENGTH: 4278
CONTENT:
## Image Digests — Registry Fundamentals and Architecture

### 1. Technical explanation

Explain the meaning, purpose, business value, main components, and where this capability fits into a container delivery platform. Clarify the difference between this concept and related ECR concepts so a beginner can understand when and why it is used.

An image digest is a content-derived identifier for an image manifest, commonly represented as a SHA-256 value. Unlike a mutable tag, the digest identifies exact manifest content. This makes it useful for reproducible deployments, artifact verification, and release traceability.

### 2. How this works in practice

After publishing an image, retrieve its digest from ECR metadata and store it with the source commit, build number, scan result, and release approval. Use the repository URI followed by @sha256:digest when deploying the exact artifact.

For this section, the engineer should understand the relationship between the selected operation and the complete ECR image lifecycle. Confirm the target AWS account, Region, repository, and image reference before performing an operation. Use the identity intended for the actual pipeline or runtime instead of relying only on an administrator account. Record the relevant resource ARN, image tag, digest, and operation result so the work can be traced later.

### 3. Practical AWS and Docker implementation

The following commands are relevant examples for this topic. Replace ACCOUNT_ID, repository names, image versions, role names, and Regions with values from the actual environment. Review commands before running any operation that changes AWS resources.

aws ecr describe-images --repository-name payments-api --region ap-south-1 --query 'imageDetails[].{Tags:imageTags,Digest:imageDigest}'
aws ecr batch-get-image --repository-name payments-api --image-ids imageTag=1.4.2 --region ap-south-1

### 4. Security and production considerations

Use digest references for production workloads where exact artifact identity matters. A digest proves content identity, not that the image is safe or trusted. Combine digest pinning with scanning, provenance, signature verification where configured, and release approval.

Production implementation should be repeatable and reviewable. Keep infrastructure configuration and IAM policies in version control. Use short-lived credentials, protect sensitive command output, and separate development and production responsibilities. Record image provenance and verify the exact artifact that is promoted. Do not treat a successful command as sufficient evidence until the resulting AWS resource or image metadata has been checked.

### 5. Troubleshooting and verification

If a digest cannot be found, verify the repository, Region, image tag, publication status, and metadata query. If a deployment uses an unexpected image, compare the deployed digest with the approved release record.

Verify the outcome by checking the AWS CLI response, repository configuration, image metadata, tag, digest, and relevant CloudTrail activity. When a failure occurs, collect the exact error message, caller identity, requested action, resource ARN, account, Region, and timestamp. Change only the configuration responsible for the failure, then repeat the operation using the same identity and environment.

### 6. DevOps pipeline application

In a CI/CD pipeline, this section should become an explicit and testable pipeline responsibility. The pipeline should validate its prerequisites, use an approved IAM role, execute the required operation, inspect the result, and stop when validation fails. Store the resulting image reference and digest with the build metadata. Pass verified artifact information to the deployment stage so that downstream environments use the intended image rather than an unverified local build.

### 7. Engineering checklist

- Confirm the ECR repository and image reference.
- Use the intended IAM identity and least-privilege permissions.
- Verify the operation using AWS metadata or Docker inspection.
- Record the image tag and digest where applicable.
- Check security, retention, and rollback requirements.
- Preserve diagnostic evidence and avoid exposing credentials.

When a failure occurs, collect the exact error message, caller identity, requested action, resource ARN, account, Region, and timestamp. Store the resulting image reference and digest with the build metadata. Pass verified artifact information to the deployment stage so that downstream environments use the intended image rather than an unverified local build.

HEADING: Lifecycle Policies — Registry Fundamentals and Architecture
CONTENT LENGTH: 4292
CONTENT:
## Lifecycle Policies — Registry Fundamentals and Architecture

### 1. Technical explanation

Explain the meaning, purpose, business value, main components, and where this capability fits into a container delivery platform. Clarify the difference between this concept and related ECR concepts so a beginner can understand when and why it is used.

ECR lifecycle policies automatically expire images according to repository rules. Rules can select images by tag status, tag prefixes, image count, or image age. Lifecycle management helps control storage growth and remove obsolete build artifacts.

### 2. How this works in practice

Define tag conventions first, then create lifecycle rules that distinguish temporary CI images from approved releases. Use lifecycle policy preview to inspect which images would be expired. Apply the policy only after confirming that required rollback artifacts are retained.

For this section, the engineer should understand the relationship between the selected operation and the complete ECR image lifecycle. Confirm the target AWS account, Region, repository, and image reference before performing an operation. Use the identity intended for the actual pipeline or runtime instead of relying only on an administrator account. Record the relevant resource ARN, image tag, digest, and operation result so the work can be traced later.

The following commands are relevant examples for this topic. Replace ACCOUNT_ID, repository names, image versions, role names, and Regions with values from the actual environment. Review commands before running any operation that changes AWS resources.

aws ecr get-lifecycle-policy --repository-name payments-api --region ap-south-1
aws ecr start-lifecycle-policy-preview --repository-name payments-api --region ap-south-1
aws ecr get-lifecycle-policy-preview --repository-name payments-api --region ap-south-1

### 4. Security and production considerations

Protect approved production images and maintain retention periods that satisfy operational and compliance needs. Store lifecycle policies in version control and review them when release frequency changes. Restrict policy changes to authorized roles.

Production implementation should be repeatable and reviewable. Keep infrastructure configuration and IAM policies in version control. Use short-lived credentials, protect sensitive command output, and separate development and production responsibilities. Record image provenance and verify the exact artifact that is promoted. Do not treat a successful command as sufficient evidence until the resulting AWS resource or image metadata has been checked.

### 5. Troubleshooting and verification

If required images disappear, inspect the lifecycle policy, rule priority, tag matching, image age, and preview results. If images are not expiring as expected, verify the rule conditions and repository policy state.

Verify the outcome by checking the AWS CLI response, repository configuration, image metadata, tag, digest, and relevant CloudTrail activity. ID: stage-9-topic-11-section-2
HEADING: Lifecycle Policies — Repository Configuration
CONTENT LENGTH: 4287
CONTENT:
## Lifecycle Policies — Repository Configuration

### 1. Technical explanation

Explain the sequence of operations from the initiating client to the AWS service and the resulting registry state. Describe the components involved, the information exchanged, the dependencies between steps, and what should happen when an individual step fails.

ECR lifecycle policies automatically expire images according to repository rules. Rules can select images by tag status, tag prefixes, image count, or image age. Lifecycle management helps control storage growth and remove obsolete build artifacts.

### 2. How this works in practice

Define tag conventions first, then create lifecycle rules that distinguish temporary CI images from approved releases. Use lifecycle policy preview to inspect which images would be expired. Apply the policy only after confirming that required rollback artifacts are retained.

For this section, the engineer should understand the relationship between the selected operation and the complete ECR image lifecycle. Confirm the target AWS account, Region, repository, and image reference before performing an operation. Use the identity intended for the actual pipeline or runtime instead of relying only on an administrator account. Record the relevant resource ARN, image tag, digest, and operation result so the work can be traced later.

### 3. Practical AWS and Docker implementation

The following commands are relevant examples for this topic. Replace ACCOUNT_ID, repository names, image versions, role names, and Regions with values from the actual environment. Review commands before running any operation that changes AWS resources.

aws ecr get-lifecycle-policy --repository-name payments-api --region ap-south-1
aws ecr start-lifecycle-policy-preview --repository-name payments-api --region ap-south-1
aws ecr get-lifecycle-policy-preview --repository-name payments-api --region ap-south-1

### 4. Security and production considerations

Protect approved production images and maintain retention periods that satisfy operational and compliance needs. Store lifecycle policies in version control and review them when release frequency changes. Restrict policy changes to authorized roles.

Production implementation should be repeatable and reviewable. Keep infrastructure configuration and IAM policies in version control. Use short-lived credentials, protect sensitive command output, and separate development and production responsibilities. Record image provenance and verify the exact artifact that is promoted. Do not treat a successful command as sufficient evidence until the resulting AWS resource or image metadata has been checked.

### 5. Troubleshooting and verification

If required images disappear, inspect the lifecycle policy, rule priority, tag matching, image age, and preview results. If images are not expiring as expected, verify the rule conditions and repository policy state.

Verify the outcome by checking the AWS CLI response, repository configuration, image metadata, tag, digest, and relevant CloudTrail activity. When a failure occurs, collect the exact error message, caller identity, requested action, resource ARN, account, Region, and timestamp. Change only the configuration responsible for the failure, then repeat the operation using the same identity and environment.

### 6. DevOps pipeline application

In a CI/CD pipeline, this section should become an explicit and testable pipeline responsibility. The pipeline should validate its prerequisites, use an approved IAM role, execute the required operation, inspect the result, and stop when validation fails. Store the resulting image reference and digest with the build metadata. Pass verified artifact information to the deployment stage so that downstream environments use the intended image rather than an unverified local build.

### 7. Engineering checklist

- Confirm the correct AWS account and Region.
- Confirm the ECR repository and image reference.
- Use the intended IAM identity and least-privilege permissions.
- Verify the operation using AWS metadata or Docker inspection.
- Record the image tag and digest where applicable.
- Check security, retention, and rollback requirements.
- Preserve diagnostic evidence and avoid exposing credentials.

Pass verified artifact information to the deployment stage so that downstream environments use the intended image rather than an unverified local build.

### 7. Engineering checklist

- Confirm the correct AWS account and Region.
- Confirm the ECR repository and image reference.
- Use the intended IAM identity and least-privilege permissions.
- Verify the operation using AWS metadata or Docker inspection.
- Record the image tag and digest where applicable.
- Check security, retention, and rollback requirements.
- Preserve diagnostic evidence and avoid exposing credentials.

HEADING: Lifecycle Policies — Replication and Availability
CONTENT LENGTH: 4291
CONTENT:
## Lifecycle Policies — Replication and Availability

### 1. Technical explanation

Explain the sequence of operations from the initiating client to the AWS service and the resulting registry state. Describe the components involved, the information exchanged, the dependencies between steps, and what should happen when an individual step fails.

ECR lifecycle policies automatically expire images according to repository rules. Rules can select images by tag status, tag prefixes, image count, or image age. Lifecycle management helps control storage growth and remove obsolete build artifacts.

### 2. How this works in practice

Define tag conventions first, then create lifecycle rules that distinguish temporary CI images from approved releases. Use lifecycle policy preview to inspect which images would be expired. Apply the policy only after confirming that required rollback artifacts are retained.

For this section, the engineer should understand the relationship between the selected operation and the complete ECR image lifecycle. Confirm the target AWS account, Region, repository, and image reference before performing an operation. Use the identity intended for the actual pipeline or runtime instead of relying only on an administrator account. Record the relevant resource ARN, image tag, digest, and operation result so the work can be traced later.

### 3. Practical AWS and Docker implementation

The following commands are relevant examples for this topic. Replace ACCOUNT_ID, repository names, image versions, role names, and Regions with values from the actual environment. Review commands before running any operation that changes AWS resources.

aws ecr get-lifecycle-policy --repository-name payments-api --region ap-south-1
aws ecr start-lifecycle-policy-preview --repository-name payments-api --region ap-south-1
aws ecr get-lifecycle-policy-preview --repository-name payments-api --region ap-south-1

### 4. Security and production considerations

Protect approved production images and maintain retention periods that satisfy operational and compliance needs. Store lifecycle policies in version control and review them when release frequency changes. Restrict policy changes to authorized roles.

Production implementation should be repeatable and reviewable. Keep infrastructure configuration and IAM policies in version control. Use short-lived credentials, protect sensitive command output, and separate development and production responsibilities. Record image provenance and verify the exact artifact that is promoted. Do not treat a successful command as sufficient evidence until the resulting AWS resource or image metadata has been checked.

### 5. Troubleshooting and verification

If required images disappear, inspect the lifecycle policy, rule priority, tag matching, image age, and preview results. If images are not expiring as expected, verify the rule conditions and repository policy state.

Verify the outcome by checking the AWS CLI response, repository configuration, image metadata, tag, digest, and relevant CloudTrail activity. When a failure occurs, collect the exact error message, caller identity, requested action, resource ARN, account, Region, and timestamp. Change only the configuration responsible for the failure, then repeat the operation using the same identity and environment.

### 6. DevOps pipeline application

In a CI/CD pipeline, this section should become an explicit and testable pipeline responsibility. The pipeline should validate its prerequisites, use an approved IAM role, execute the required operation, inspect the result, and stop when validation fails. Store the resulting image reference and digest with the build metadata.
